title: Algorithmic Design Of Heralded Linear Optical Circuits For Multipartite Entanglement
authors: Jaehee Kim, Hon Wai Lau, William J. Munro, Joonsuk Huh, Seungbeom Chin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heralded multipartite entanglement is a key resource for various quantum information tasks. However, designing linear optical circuits that generate specific target states is generally challenging due to the complexity of the required optical structures. Here we formulate the design of heralded photonic circuits as an algorithmic graph-search problem. Our framework enables the automated construction and optimization of heralded photonic circuits by substantially reducing the search space using the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture. Our strategy reconstructs circuit structures as graphs in the picture and identifies suitable graphs automatically. As a result, we design efficient schemes for a broad range of useful multipartite resource states, including hypergraph magic states, quantum error correcting codes, general three-qubit states and length-1 caterpillar graph states. Our work establishes an algorithmic framework for the systematic discovery of heralded resource states, laying the foundation for the automated design of increasingly complex multipartite entangled resources.
tldr: The paper formulates the design of heralded linear optical circuits for multipartite entanglement as an algorithmic graph-search problem, enabling automated construction of resource states.
motivation: Heralded multipartite entanglement is a key resource for quantum information tasks, but designing linear optical circuits to generate specific target states is challenging due to the complexity of optical structures.
method: The authors use the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture to reduce the search space, reconstruct circuit structures as graphs, and automatically identify suitable graphs via graph search.
result: The framework designs efficient schemes for a broad range of resource states, including hypergraph magic states, quantum error correcting codes, general three-qubit states, and length-1 caterpillar graph states.
conclusion: This work establishes an algorithmic framework for systematic discovery of heralded resource states, laying the foundation for automated design of increasingly complex multipartite entangled resources.

title: Quantifying And Bounding Spatiotemporal Correlations In Quantum Noise
authors: Diogo O. Soares-Pinto Guilherme Zambon
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial and temporal correlations in quantum noise challenge the local Markovian models commonly used in quantum information processing. We develop a unified operational framework for quantifying temporal, spatial, and total spatiotemporal correlations in general quantum processes. Using process tensors, we define these quantities through optimal distinguishability from Markovian, spatially local, and fully uncorrelated processes. Optimization over admissible probing combs ensures monotonicity under every superprocess that preserves the corresponding free set, while Choi-state functionals and restricted probes provide accessible lower bounds. We establish hierarchy and interpolation relations among the correlation measures and derive dimension-dependent upper bounds on temporal correlations transmitted by quantum memories, with tighter bounds for classical memory, together with universal ceilings imposed by the system dimension. These bounds turn certified lower estimates into witnesses of minimum memory dimension, nonclassicality under a memory-dimension constraint, and inconsistencies in the assumed process model. We illustrate the results with effective superconducting-qubit models featuring \(ZZ\) and \(XY\) interactions, exhibiting saturation of classical-memory, quantum-memory, and system-dimension ceilings. These results pave the way toward practical approaches to characterizing and addressing spatiotemporally correlated errors in quantum devices.
tldr: The paper develops a unified operational framework using process tensors to quantify and bound spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal correlations in quantum noise, with applications to certifying memory dimension and nonclassicality.
motivation: Local Markovian models are inadequate for describing correlated quantum noise in quantum devices, so a framework to quantify and bound spatiotemporal correlations is needed.
method: They define correlation measures via optimal distinguishability from Markovian, spatially local, or uncorrelated processes using process tensors, probing combs, and Choi-state functionals to derive monotonicity and lower bounds.
result: They establish hierarchy and interpolation relations, dimension-dependent upper bounds on temporal correlations transmittable through quantum channels, and operational witnesses for non-Markovianity and memory dimension.

title: The Quantum Mpemba Effect In Symmetric Random Clifford Circuits
authors: Shion Yamashika, Filiberto Ares, Pasquale Calabrese
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum Mpemba effect is the counterintuitive phenomenon whereby a quantum state initially farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one initially closer to it. We demonstrate this effect in random Clifford circuits with a conserved [MATH] charge, using the entanglement asymmetry to characterize relaxation through dynamical symmetry restoration. Exact numerical simulations show that an initially more asymmetric state can become locally more symmetric than an initially less asymmetric one. We explain this behavior by mapping the dynamics onto a charge-conserving quantum automaton, in which the decay of the entanglement asymmetry is controlled by the statistics of encounters between two particle species evolving according to a symmetric simple exclusion process. This mapping yields an analytic expression for the entanglement asymmetry and provides a simple microscopic mechanism for the quantum Mpemba effect: stronger initial symmetry breaking corresponds to a denser particle configuration, which enhances the frequency of particle encounters and thereby accelerates symmetry restoration.

motivation: The quantum Mpemba effect—faster relaxation from states farther from equilibrium—is counterintuitive and relevant to non-equilibrium quantum dynamics and symmetry restoration. title: Remote Adiabatic Controlled-Z Gate Between Distant Superconducting Qubits

abstract: ArXiv:2609.18081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Direct entangling gates between spatially separated qubits are a key capability for modular quantum computing. abstract: ArXiv:2609.18195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear--quadratic--Gaussian (LQG) control is optimal only with respect to a prescribed cost function, the choice of which dictates the physical objective of the control. title: The Golden Junction Of Gaussian Covariance Geometries: Sector Anisotropy, Relative-Entropy Response, And Local Penalties

abstract: ArXiv:2609.17574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We compare four local geometries of centered one-mode bosonic Gaussian covariances while keeping their operational meanings distinct. title: Structure Of Measurement-Induced Entanglement In Infinite-Randomness Critical States
authors: Oliver Breach
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The impact of projective measurements on a many-body quantum state is tightly linked to its underlying entanglement structure. Critical states are particularly sensitive, as long-range entanglement allows local measurements to have global consequences. This has been extensively studied in the context of critical states described by a conformal field theory (CFT), where measurements can alter critical properties in post-measurement quantities ('measurement-altered criticality') and induce long-range entanglement with universal features ('measurement-induced entanglement'). By contrast, little is known about the role of measurements on critical states with quenched disorder, which admit no CFT description. Here, we develop a theory of measurements on one-dimensional critical states governed by infinite-randomness fixed points (IRFPs), focusing on two closely related examples: the random XXZ chain and the random transverse-field Ising model. We show that the measurement-induced entanglement decays as a power-law with universal exponent [MATH] in both models, and that the minimum number of measurements required to establish this entanglement obeys a universal scaling form. When only a finite density of measurements is made, we show that the critical properties of the state are remarkably robust: `measurement-altered criticality' is absent, with measurements either preserving the critical exponents, or destroying the criticality entirely. These results establish IRFPs as an analytically tractable arena for measurements on critical states, complementary to the CFT case. The outcome randomness that necessitates replica methods in clean systems becomes trivial at infinite randomness, with the universal response governed by the statistics induced by the quenched disorder.

conclusion: Infinite-randomness fixed points provide an analytically tractable complementary arena to CFT for studying measurements on critical states, with universal response governed by quenched-disorder statistics.

title: R\'enyi And Tsallis Information Entropies For A Harmonic Position-dependent Mass

abstract: ArXiv:2609.17941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study Renyi and Tsallis information entropies for a Hamiltonian system with position-dependent mass confined in harmonic oscillator potential. Finally, we evaluate the related entropic uncertainty relations numerically to validate the latter obersevations.

abstract: ArXiv:2609.17979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating quantum state properties is essential across a wide range of applications, from studying quantum many-body physics to benchmarking quantum hardware. Furthermore, we report results obtained from a superconducting quantum processor developed by Academia Sinica and analyzed using the standalone estimation workflow. title: Quantum Encodings, Private Messages, And Communication Complexity
authors: Tom Gur, Miryam Mi-Ying Huang, Er-Cheng Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the complexity of quantum decomposable randomized encodings (QDRE). We establish a bi-directional connection between the QDRE model and the communication complexity model of quantum private simultaneous message protocols (QPSM), where classical communication is free, and quantum communication is the primary complexity measure. We show the following upper and lower bounds. (1) For every quantum channel mapping [MATH] to [MATH] qubits, we give a QPSM protocol with quantum communication [MATH], using exponential pre-shared entanglement. In particular, constant-output channels have [MATH] quantum communication, and classical-output channels require no quantum communication. (2) With [MATH] pre-shared entanglement, every one-qubit-output channel has an [MATH]-quantum-communication QPSM protocol. Conversely, there exists a channel and a constant [MATH] for which any protocol with at most [MATH] pre-shared entanglement requires [MATH] quantum communication. (3) In contrast, we identify a structured class of quantum channels, Clifford-induced channels, for which there exist QPSM protocols with [MATH] pre-shared entangled qubits and only [MATH] quantum communication complexity. Through our connection, we obtain analogous upper and lower bounds on the quantum encoding size of QDRE. Our results show that the amount of pre-shared entanglement plays a central role in quantum encoding size and quantum communication complexity.
tldr: The paper establishes a bidirectional connection between quantum decomposable randomized encodings (QDRE) and quantum private simultaneous message protocols (QPSM), deriving upper and lower bounds on quantum communication and encoding size.
motivation: To understand how quantum communication and pre-shared entanglement affect the complexity of randomized encodings and private simultaneous message protocols.
method: It links the QDRE model to QPSM with free classical communication, then proves protocols and lower bounds for general and Clifford-induced quantum channels.
result: It shows exponential pre-shared entanglement enables efficient protocols for general channels, one-qubit-output channels need little entanglement, but some channels require linear quantum communication; Clifford-induced channels achieve linear entanglement and logarithmic communication.
conclusion: Pre-shared entanglement plays a central role in quantum encoding size and quantum communication complexity, with structured channels admitting better trade-offs.

title: Efficiency-Resolved Recovery Dynamics Of An Free-Running InGaAs/InP Single Photon Avalanche Detector Operated In Gated Mode
authors: Bruno Santos Souza, Vitor Tavares, Filippo Ghiglieno, Celso Jorge Villas-Boas, Paulo Henrique Dias Ferreira
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Detection efficiency in gated-mode single-photon avalanche detectors recovers gradually after each gate edge, limiting attainable count rates, yet quantitative recovery models exist only for free-running operation. We extract the gated recovery time constant of a free-running InGaAs/InP detector at 1550 nm by sweeping the gate frequency from 100 kHz to 1 MHz and globally fitting count rates across four dead times, requiring neither a pulsed laser nor a time-to-digital converter. The recovery time decreases linearly with detection efficiency, from 301 to 161 ns between 10 % and 25 %, at 9.3 ns per percentage point. We further resolve a periodic count-rate modulation consistent with bias-dependent capacitive gate feedthrough.
tldr: The paper extracts the gated recovery time constant of a free-running InGaAs/InP single-photon avalanche detector by sweeping gate frequency and globally fitting count rates across dead times.
motivation: Detection efficiency in gated-mode single-photon avalanche detectors recovers gradually after each gate edge, limiting attainable count rates, but quantitative recovery models existed only for free-running operation.
method: The authors sweep gate frequency from 100 kHz to 1 MHz and globally fit count rates across four dead times, requiring neither a pulsed laser nor a time-to-digital converter.
result: The recovery time decreases linearly with detection efficiency, from 301 to 161 ns between 10% and 25%, at 9.3 ns per percentage point; a periodic count-rate modulation is consistent with bias-dependent capacitive gate feedthrough.
conclusion: The work provides a quantitative gated recovery model for free-running InGaAs/InP detectors, which may aid optimization of high-rate single-photon detection in quantum communication.

title: Fourier Analysis Of Parametrized Interactive Quantum Classifiers
authors: F\'abio Novaes, Fernando M. de Paula Neto, Jo\~ao V. M. Cardoso
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactive Quantum Classifiers (IQCs) constitute a family of quantum machine learning models inspired by open quantum systems, in which the interaction between a target qubit and an environment is described by a Hamiltonian. Previous works introduced alternative Hamiltonian parameterizations and showed empirically that they can improve classification performance, but the role of these parameters in the resulting classifier remains poorly understood. In this work, we derive a closed-form expression for the reduced quantum channel generated by a parametrized IQC with a single target qubit. The analytical solution explicitly reveals how the Hamiltonian parameters control the constant, sine, and cosine components of the classifier output, establishing a Fourier interpretation of the induced feature map. This analysis motivates a generalized family of Hamiltonian encodings, including matrix-parameterized environmental Hamiltonians whose Fourier components depend on linear combinations of input features, thereby enabling non-separable Fourier structures. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the proposed models can improve classification performance on several nonlinear benchmarks. The generalized matrix encoding achieves the strongest aggregate performance in the evaluated benchmark, while a simpler four-parameter extension often attains comparable performance with substantially fewer trainable parameters. We additionally characterize the generated state ensembles using the standard fidelity-based expressibility measure, finding that global expressibility does not directly predict classification performance. Our results provide an analytical characterization of parametrized Hamiltonians in Interactive Quantum Classifiers and establish Fourier analysis as a useful framework for understanding and designing open-system-inspired quantum learning models.
tldr: The paper derives a closed-form expression for the reduced quantum channel of a parametrized Interactive Quantum Classifier, showing that Hamiltonian parameters control Fourier (constant, sine, cosine) components of the output, and uses this to motivate generalized matrix-parameterized encodings.
motivation: Previous work showed that alternative Hamiltonian parameterizations empirically improve classification in Interactive Quantum Classifiers, but the functional role of these parameters was poorly understood, lacking a principled analytical characterization.
method: The authors analytically solve for the reduced channel of a single-target-qubit IQC interacting with a Hamiltonian-described environment, extracting the Fourier structure of the induced feature map and generalizing to matrix-parameterized environmental Hamiltonians enabling non-separable Fourier features; numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets plus fidelity-based expressibility measures validate the analysis.
result: The generalized matrix encoding achieves the strongest aggregate classification performance, while a simpler four-parameter extension often matches it with far fewer trainable parameters; global expressibility does not directly predict classification performance.
conclusion: Fourier analysis provides a useful framework for understanding and designing parametrized Hamiltonians in open-system-inspired quantum learning models, though the work remains an applied quantum machine learning contribution rather than an information-theoretic one.

title: Logarithmic Singularity In A Dynamical Quantum Phase Transition For Free Fermions
authors: Yasser Bezzaz, Dimitri M. Gangardt, Pavel L. Krapivsky, Jean-Marc Luck, Kirone Mallick, Sylvain Prolhac
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the Loschmidt echo in a system of N non-interacting spinless lattice fermions released from a double-domain-wall initial state. In the large-N limit, the return probability is characterized by a large-deviation rate function known as the dynamical free energy. The Loschmidt echo is dominated by a complex instanton configuration, and the dynamical free energy develops a logarithmic singularity at the dynamical quantum phase transition. We obtain analytical results in the short-time and long-time regimes and support them with numerical computations. We show that the transition can be understood as a topological change of the dominant instanton configuration, analogous to the emergence of a cut in random matrix theory. We further show that post-selection can drive the system through two successive DQPTs, associated with successive topological changes of the dominant instanton configuration in complex time.
tldr: The paper studies the Loschmidt echo in free fermions from a double-domain-wall initial state, finding a logarithmic singularity at a dynamical quantum phase transition interpreted as a topological change of the dominant instanton.
motivation: Dynamical quantum phase transitions and Loschmidt echoes are key to understanding non-equilibrium quantum many-body dynamics, but their analytical characterization in free-fermion systems remains incomplete.
method: Using the large-N limit, the return probability is expressed via a large-deviation rate function (dynamical free energy). The authors identify the dominant complex instanton configuration, obtain analytical results in short- and long-time regimes, and support them with numerical computations.
result: The dynamical free energy exhibits a logarithmic singularity at the transition, which corresponds to a topological change in the dominant instanton configuration, analogous to a cut in random matrix theory. Post-selection can drive the system through two successive DQPTs.
conclusion: The work provides a detailed analytical and numerical understanding of DQPTs in free fermions, linking the transition to instanton topology and highlighting the role of post-selection.

title: Entropy Estimates From Stochastic Interpolants
authors: Phillip M. Rauscher
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a general method for estimating entropy differences between arbitrary probability distributions using stochastic interpolants. The marginal distributions which bridge the base and target obey a continuity equation, which allows a straightforward calculation of the entropy difference in terms of an inner product of the probability flow velocity and score fields. This formulation has several advantages: (i) no computationally expensive divergence calculations of either field are required, (ii) the score field need not even be learned directly if model transferability is not required, and (iii) on-the-fly estimates are produced nearly for free during training. When tractable base distributions are chosen (e.g. Gaussian chain, ideal gas, etc.), statistical thermodynamic entropies are then immediately recovered. Notably, the analysis relies only on the definition of the Gibbs-Shannon entropy, rather than any particular statistical mechanical ensemble, so that generalized non-equilibrium entropies may be computed. The method is demonstrated on several systems of increasing complexity: (i) a 40-dimensional Gaussian mixture model, (ii) the classical XY model of N spins arranged in one dimension, (iii) the 13-atom Lennard-Jones cluster, and (iv) an active Brownian polymer.
tldr: A method to estimate entropy differences between arbitrary probability distributions using stochastic interpolants, requiring only score and velocity fields along the interpolating path.
motivation: Entropy estimation in high-dimensional or strongly interacting systems is computationally challenging, often requiring expensive divergence calculations or full density estimation.
method: Stochastic interpolants bridge a tractable base distribution and a target distribution via a continuity equation; the entropy difference is expressed as an inner product of the probability flow velocity and score fields, avoiding divergence computations.
result: The method yields on-the-fly entropy estimates during training and is demonstrated on a 40-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the classical XY model, a 13-atom Lennard-Jones cluster, and an active Brownian polymer.
conclusion: By relying only on the Gibbs-Shannon entropy, the approach recovers statistical thermodynamic entropies and enables computation of generalized non-equilibrium entropies for classical systems.

title: Second-Order Asymptotics For The Gaussian Mac On The Relative Interior Of The Sum-Rate Face
authors: Vincent Y. F. Tan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We completely characterize the second-order coding rate region of the two-user Gaussian multiple-access channel at points in the relative interior of the sum-rate face, under maximal per-codeword power constraints. For any fixed average error probability [MATH], a nontrivial mixture of power splits reduces the sum-rate dispersion and strictly improves upon standard inner bounds based on a constant power split. Thus, a constant power split, although sufficient to attain the first-order capacity region, is insufficient for second-order optimality in this regime. Our achievability proof builds on the constant composition and coded time-sharing framework of Scarlett, Martinez, and Guill\'en i F\`abregas, with an optimization over admissible power splits. A matching second-order converse establishes the optimality of the resulting coded time-sharing strategy.
tldr: The paper completely characterizes the second-order coding rate region of the two-user Gaussian multiple-access channel on the relative interior of the sum-rate face, showing that a non-constant power split outperforms a constant power split for second-order optimality.
motivation: While a constant power split is optimal for first-order (capacity) performance, the second-order analysis reveals that varying power allocation can improve the trade-off between rates.

title: QEMScore: How Much Does The Measurement Add To Learned Quantum Error Mitigation?
authors: Yue Zhao, Huayue Gu, Yushun Dong, Xiyang Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much does the noisy measurement add to learned quantum error mitigation? An accuracy table cannot say, because a model handed circuit structure can score well without reading the measurement at all. QEMScore adds the comparison that can. Each simulated circuit carries an exact ideal answer. The learned mitigator is scored beside a capacity-matched control, a model just as flexible that reads the same circuit description but never the measurement. Each method's measurement spend is accounted and not equalized. We run a controlled campaign on simulated circuits and reanalyze two published learned mitigators, Q-LEAR and QRAFT, from their released hardware data. Three findings stand out. First, under familiar within-family conditions (S0) evaluated across two spin-chain families and three seeds, continuous couplings identify the target, and the control that never reads the measurement matches 87.7 to 100.5 percent of the mitigator's gain over an affine fit to the circuit description. A plain polynomial in the coupling parameters, fitted after the campaign, beats the mitigator on all six evaluations, reflecting the selected learners' capacity. Second, for these selected learners, matching most of the gain is not matching the accuracy: on five of six evaluations the mitigator removes 19.5 to 74.5 percent of the error the capacity-matched control leaves, a learner-specific gap rather than a measurement requirement. Third, on released hardware data where descriptors only partially identify queries, the findings differ: flexible models of the descriptors show negligible mean gain over affine fits in Q-LEAR, and measurement inputs carry predictive gains in both Q-LEAR and QRAFT. These comparisons reflect representation- and protocol-specific behavior rather than an isolated cross-regime difference. A learned mitigator's accuracy should therefore be reported beside such controls.
tldr: QEMScore evaluates learned quantum error mitigation by comparing it to a capacity-matched control that ignores measurement, revealing that apparent gains often come from circuit description rather than measurement data.
motivation: Standard accuracy metrics cannot isolate whether a learned mitigator actually uses measurement information or merely exploits circuit structure, so a controlled comparison is needed.
method: The authors score learned mitigators alongside capacity-matched controls that read the same circuit description but no measurement, account for measurement spend, run simulated spin-chain experiments, and reanalyze Q-LEAR and QRAFT hardware data.
result: In within-family simulations, controls match 87.7–100.5% of the mitigator's gain and a simple polynomial beats the mitigator on all six evaluations; on hardware, measurement inputs show predictive gains for Q-LEAR and QRAFT, though descriptor-only flexible models yield negligible gain over affine fits for Q-LEAR.
conclusion: Measurement contribution to learned QEM is learner- and regime-specific, so reported accuracies should be accompanied by capacity-matched controls to establish genuine measurement utility.

title: Depth Analysis Of The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm With A Grover Mixer
authors: Dimitar Grantcharov Bojko N. Bakalov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm with a Grover mixer and independently sampled cost and mixing angles. Under a lattice condition on the cost values carried by the initial state, we prove a depth-independent lower bound for the variance of the loss at every depth, together with the same bound for the derivative with respect to the final mixing angle. The estimate is instance-dependent and, for fixed locality, is inverse polynomial in the number of qubits for integer-valued local objective functions with uniformly bounded local terms, in particular for MaxCut. We also establish Grover-type reachability bounds showing that the depth required to approximate a prescribed carried eigenspace is bounded below by a constant multiple of the inverse square root of its initial probability.
tldr: We prove depth-independent lower bounds on the loss variance and its derivative for QAOA with a Grover mixer, and derive Grover-type reachability bounds on the required depth.
motivation: Understanding the depth requirements and trainability of variational quantum algorithms like QAOA is crucial for assessing their practical utility on near-term quantum devices.
method: Under a lattice condition on the cost values, analytical proofs establish instance-dependent lower bounds for the variance of the loss and its derivative with respect to the final mixing angle, as well as reachability bounds for approximating a prescribed eigenspace.
result: For fixed locality, the lower bound is inverse polynomial in the number of qubits for integer-valued local objective functions with uniformly bounded local terms, including MaxCut; the depth needed to approximate an eigenspace is bounded below by a constant times the inverse square root of its initial probability.
conclusion: The analysis provides theoretical guarantees on depth and trainability for Grover-mixer QAOA, highlighting fundamental limitations that are largely orthogonal to the researcher's interests in quantum information theory, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems.

title: Hyper-derivative Algebraic Geometry Codes Via Local Expansions
authors: Xiaofeng Liu, Hengfeng Liu, Jun Zhang, Fang-Wei Fu, Chunming Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we develop a systematic construction framework of hyper-derivative algebraic geometry codes via local expansions, extending hyper-derivative Reed-Solomon codes from the rational function field to general algebraic function fields. Using the residue theorem, we determine their Euclidean duals and illustrate that the duals naturally reverse. We further give criteria for reverse self orthogonality and reverse self duality in terms of two classes of bilinear forms. Finally, we provide an asymptotic bound on the rate and relative distance via function field towers.
tldr: The paper constructs hyper-derivative algebraic geometry codes via local expansions on general function fields and analyzes their duals and asymptotic performance.
motivation: Hyper-derivative Reed-Solomon codes have been studied on the rational function field, but a general construction on arbitrary algebraic function fields was lacking.
method: Using local expansions and the residue theorem, the authors determine the Euclidean duals of these codes and derive criteria for reverse self-orthogonality and reverse self-duality via two classes of bilinear forms.
result: They establish that duals naturally reverse, provide criteria for self-duality properties, and obtain an asymptotic bound on rate and relative distance using function field towers.
conclusion: This provides a systematic framework for hyper-derivative AG codes and extends the theory beyond rational function fields.

title: The Expressive Power Of Constrained Qaoa: What You Might Have MISsed
authors: Boris Tsvelikhovskiy, Bao Bach, Ilya Safro
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Feasibility-preserving mixer Hamiltonians offer an attractive alternative to penalty encodings for constrained quantum optimization, yet how enforcing constraints alters the state space reachable by the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) remains largely unexplored. We address this question within the context of the Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem. Alongside the standard controlled bit-flip mixer, we analyze the alternative [MATH] mixer, whose restriction to the feasible subspace [MATH] corresponds precisely to the shifted negative Laplacian of the independent-set reconfiguration graph. Although both mixers induce identical transitions between independent sets, the diagonal modification changes the spectral structure and can substantially enlarge the set of reachable quantum states. For every connected input graph with at least two vertices, we prove that independently parameterized local controls associated with either mixer generate the full unitary Lie algebra on the feasible subspace. Standard QAOA exhibits a more nuanced algebraic structure. We prove that the dynamical Lie algebra associated with MIS-QAOA employing the conventional mixer embeds into its Flip-or-Stay counterpart. Furthermore, we construct an infinite family of graphs for which the corresponding vacuum-state dynamical group orbits exhibit strictly distinct dimensions, establishing a qualitative expressivity separation between the two architectures. For either mixer, we show that standard QAOA initialized in the empty set can prepare a state supported entirely on maximum independent sets at finite depth. For the free architectures, we also derive an exact loss-variance formula in the unitary-design limit, expressed through the number of feasible independent sets and the variance of their cardinalities.
tldr: The paper analyzes the dynamical Lie algebras and reachable state spaces of constrained QAOA for Maximum Independent Set, comparing a standard controlled bit-flip mixer with a Laplacian-based alternative mixer.
motivation: Feasibility-preserving mixer Hamiltonians are an appealing alternative to penalty encodings for constrained quantum optimization, but how constraint enforcement reshapes QAOA's reachable state space is poorly understood.
method: Working on the feasible subspace of the MIS problem, the authors compare the conventional controlled bit-flip mixer with a shifted-negative-Laplacian 'Flip-or-Stay' mixer, using dynamical Lie algebra and group-orbit arguments plus a loss-variance analysis in the unitary-design limit.
result: Local controls with either mixer generate the full unitary Lie algebra on the feasible subspace; the standard QAOA Lie algebra embeds into its Flip-or-Stay counterpart, and an infinite family of graphs exhibits strictly distinct vacuum-orbit dimensions, giving a qualitative expressivity separation. Standard QAOA from the empty state can also prepare states supported only on maximum independent sets at finite depth.
conclusion: Constraint-preserving mixer choice materially affects QAOA's expressive power, with the Laplacian-type mixer generally offering larger reachable state spaces, though the work is a theoretical quantum-algorithms study rather than an information-theoretic result.

title: A Global Readiness And Sovereignty Capability Model For Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration
authors: Mohamed Aly Bouke
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cryptographic dependence predates the quantum era, but the migration to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) opens a rare window to reshape it, because the algorithms, implementations, hardware, and standards adopted now can lock in dependence or sovereignty for decades. This paper introduces the Readiness-Sovereignty Capability Model (RSCM), a national measurement model that operationalizes PQC readiness together with cryptographic sovereignty, which current maturity models score only as readiness and the sovereignty literature defines without measuring. RSCM decomposes sovereignty into three distinct constructs, indigenous cryptographic capacity, indigenous post-quantum control, and external dependency, and certifies a post-quantum maker only through a gate requiring demonstrated, institutionally sustained creation in at least one core layer, whether design, implementation, or validation. Applying it to fifty-seven documented cryptographic actors coded from cited public evidence, and testing that coding with an independent second coder, a plausible-state bootstrap, and convergent-validity checks, we find that twenty countries clear the gate, fifteen as full-stack makers and five as research makers, eleven hold strong general capacity without post-quantum control, one is a ready adopter, and twenty-five are dependent. The gate cells show substantial weighted agreement, a quadratic-weighted kappa of 0.71, and the maker classification is stable in its core though uncertain at the threshold. Readiness tracks independent cyber indices at rank correlations up to 0.70, while post-quantum creation shows no significant correlation with the commitment index, a rank correlation of only 0.22 that separates control from readiness. The paper contributes the framework, the evidence-graded assessment, and policy directions for building indigenous quantum-safe capacity.
tldr: The paper introduces a national Readiness-Sovereignty Capability Model (RSCM) to measure post-quantum cryptography migration readiness and cryptographic sovereignty.
motivation: The migration to post-quantum cryptography offers a rare window to reshape cryptographic dependence, yet current maturity models treat readiness and sovereignty as the same thing and sovereignty literature lacks measurement.
method: RSCM decomposes sovereignty into indigenous cryptographic capacity, indigenous post-quantum control, and external dependency, then applies a gate-based certification to 57 documented cryptographic actors using independent second coding, plausible-state bootstrap, and convergent-validity checks.
result: Twenty countries clear the gate (15 full-stack makers, 5 research makers), with substantial weighted agreement (quadratic-weighted kappa 0.71); readiness correlates with independent cyber indices up to 0.70, while post-quantum creation shows only 0.22 rank correlation with a commitment index.
conclusion: The framework provides an evidence-graded assessment and policy directions for building indigenous quantum-safe capacity, separating post-quantum control from general readiness.

title: A Polynomial-Time Attack On The McEliece Cryptosystem On Elliptic Codes With Arbitrary Divisors
authors: Artyom Kuninets, Ekaterina Malygina, Evgeniy Melnichuk
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The McEliece cryptosystem based on algebraic geometry codes has been proposed as a way to reduce the key size of code-based cryptography, but several structural attacks have demonstrated the vulnerability of particular families of algebraic geometry codes. Despite this, until recently, there remained schemes and parameter sets that were not vulnerable to any known attack. We propose a new structural attack with ``hints'' that applies to elliptic codes with arbitrary effective divisors. In particular, we prove that, given the elliptic curve, the public generator matrix, and three points from the evaluation divisor, the entire divisor can be recovered in polynomial time, independently of the number of errors used in the cryptosystem. The attack requires [MATH] operations in [MATH] and succeeds with overwhelming probability, after which the second divisor is recovered in [MATH] operations. We further propose an optimized version of the attack that requires no additional information at all. Exploiting the action of the automorphisms of the curve, the three known points are replaced by the enumeration of a single pair of field elements, which yields an equivalent key on the given public curve in [MATH] operations on average.
tldr: The paper presents a polynomial-time structural attack recovering the secret divisor of McEliece-type cryptosystems built on elliptic algebraic geometry codes, including a hint-free optimized variant.
motivation: Algebraic geometry codes were proposed to shrink key sizes in code-based cryptography, and although many families have been broken by structural attacks, some elliptic-code parameter sets remained secure against all known attacks.
method: Given the elliptic curve, the public generator matrix, and three points of the evaluation divisor, the authors exploit the geometry of elliptic codes to reconstruct the entire divisor in polynomial time via linear algebra over the base field, and further use curve automorphisms to eliminate the need for known points.
result: The attack recovers the first divisor in polynomial time independently of the number of injected errors and succeeds with overwhelming probability, with the second divisor recovered in a further polynomial number of operations; the hint-free version yields an equivalent key in polynomial time on average.
conclusion: The work breaks a previously unbroken class of elliptic-code McEliece variants, showing such parameter sets are insecure and cautioning against algebraic geometry codes with arbitrary effective divisors for post-quantum cryptography.

title: Information Spectrum Methods For $\varepsilon$-Capacity Problems In The Theory Of Mixed Multiple-Access Channels With Cost Constraint
authors: Hideki Yagi Te Sun Han
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the [MATH]-capacity regions of mixed multiple-access channels (MACs) with general mixture where the channel inputs are subject to a cost constraint. We first determine the [MATH]-capacity results for additive MACs. We next give a single-letterized inner bound on the [MATH]-capacity region for mixed memoryless MACs, and furthermore establish a single-letterized [MATH]-capacity region of the mixed memoryless MAC with finite alphabets in terms of the essential infimum of mutual informations for component channels. We also show that the Gaussian MAC with additive Gaussian noise satisfies the strong converse property, which is stronger than the traditional strong converse theorem, via a simple proof based on the information spectrum method that does not require the well-known ``wringing'' technique. We then focus on the quasi-static fading Gaussian MAC, for which we derive the [MATH]-capacity region and show that it, in the case specialized to single-users, exactly coincides with the traditional [MATH]-outage capacity region, thereby providing a Shannon-theoretic operational interpretation of the latter. We further verify, via the information spectrum method, that the [MATH]-capacity regions coincide across four scenarios of CSI availability (no-CSI, CSIR, CSIT, and CSIRT). We also demonstrate that this coincidence generally fails for mixed MACs with general (not necessarily stationary or ergodic) components, and give a counter example to prove it. Finally, we extend these results to the [MATH]-user quasi-static fading Gaussian MAC.
tldr: The paper uses information spectrum methods to characterize ε-capacity regions for mixed multiple-access channels with cost constraints, including Gaussian and quasi-static fading cases.
motivation: ε-capacity (capacity with a tolerated error probability) for channels with mixed/compound components and input cost constraints is not fully understood, especially for multi-user settings like the MAC.
method: Information spectrum methods are applied to derive single-letterized inner and outer bounds on ε-capacity regions, with a simple proof of the strong converse property for the Gaussian MAC avoiding the 'wringing' technique.
result: Exact single-letter ε-capacity regions are established for mixed memoryless MACs with finite alphabets, and the ε-capacity region for the quasi-static fading Gaussian MAC coincides with the traditional ε-outage capacity region, with CSI-independence verified across four scenarios.
conclusion: The results provide a Shannon-theoretic operational interpretation of outage capacity and demonstrate that CSI-invariance breaks down for general non-stationary/non-ergodic mixed MACs, with an explicit counterexample.

title: Machine Learning Kinetics From Molecular Dynamics Data
authors: Aaron R. Dinner Jonathan Weare
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most molecular transitions occur on timescales far beyond direct molecular dynamics simulations. The committor, the probability that a configuration reaches a product state before a reactant state, is a central kinetic statistic, providing a mechanism-independent reaction coordinate and a foundation for transition path theory and the calculation of rates. This review surveys modern approaches for estimating the committor and related kinetic statistics from molecular simulations, with an emphasis on self-supervised methods that learn solutions of their defining dynamical equations rather than relying on labeled shooting data. We develop a common operator viewpoint connecting generator-based partial differential equations, variational principles, Markov state models, dynamical Galerkin approximation, and neural networks. Empirical and theoretical evidence points to the efficiency of these methods. We provide theoretical and practical guidance for realizing their full potential in applications, including strategies for treating non-Markovian effects and for sampling. We conclude by identifying opportunities for further research, including connections to reinforcement learning and generative modeling.
tldr: A review of modern machine-learning and self-supervised approaches for estimating the committor and kinetic statistics from molecular dynamics data, unified through an operator viewpoint.
motivation: Most molecular transitions occur on timescales far beyond direct molecular dynamics simulations, so efficient estimation of kinetic statistics like the committor is essential for understanding reaction mechanisms and rates.
method: The authors survey self-supervised methods that learn solutions of the committor's defining dynamical equations, connecting generator-based PDEs, variational principles, Markov state models, dynamical Galerkin approximation, and neural networks.
result: Empirical and theoretical evidence indicates these methods are efficient, and the review offers theoretical and practical guidance on treating non-Markovian effects and sampling issues.
conclusion: The review identifies open opportunities, including connections to reinforcement learning and generative modeling, for advancing committor estimation.

title: Counterexample To A Proposed Capacity Characterization Of The Relay Channel
authors: Chun Hei Michael Shiu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18727v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a counterexample to the relay channel capacity characterization proposed in a recent work, which is based on properties of typical sequences. The counterexample uses a binary relay channel with a noiseless source-destination component and binary symmetric relay links. An achievable scheme exceeds the proposed capacity characterization, thereby disproving the characterization of the capacity for general relay channels. We highlight that the counterexample is obtained with the assistance of ChatGPT-6 Astra and the proofs are simplified with human effort.
tldr: The paper constructs a binary relay channel counterexample that refutes a recently proposed capacity characterization for general relay channels.
motivation: A recent work proposed a capacity characterization for the general relay channel based on typical-sequence properties, and the author aims to test whether that characterization is actually correct.
method: A binary relay channel with a noiseless source-destination link and binary symmetric relay links is analyzed, and an achievable coding scheme is exhibited that exceeds the proposed capacity region (with proof assistance from an LLM).
result: The achievable rate exceeds the proposed capacity characterization, providing a concrete counterexample that disproves the claimed general relay channel capacity formula.
conclusion: The proposed typical-sequence-based capacity characterization for general relay channels is invalid; classical relay channel capacity remains an open problem.

title: The 3/4 Conjecture For q-Ary Fix-Free Codes With At Most Three Distinct Codeword Lengths
authors: Zhi Shan Weiguo Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18237v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the \(3/4\) conjecture for \(q\)-ary fix-free codes with at most three distinct codeword lengths, for every integer \(q\geq2\). Every prescribed length distribution with Kraft sum at most \(3/4\) is realized by a deterministic construction. We introduce a matrix approach based on an exact identity for the overlap between forbidden prefix extensions and suffix residuals. Natural numerical order fixes the shortest layer, and the remaining selection problem is expressed through row and column counts. A fixed-cardinality interpolation theorem supplies feasible sets of every intermediate cardinality between nested endpoints, provided their differences satisfy one-sided uniqueness and either acyclicity or integral slack. Reverse-order selection handles the uniform cases directly; in the remaining cases, layer completion and aligned groups provide endpoints for interpolation. Together, these methods extend the binary three-length result to arbitrary finite alphabets and give a deterministic procedure for constructing the code.
tldr: The paper proves the 3/4 conjecture for q-ary fix-free codes with at most three distinct codeword lengths, extending a binary result via a deterministic construction.
motivation: The 3/4 conjecture asks whether any length distribution with Kraft sum at most 3/4 can be realized by a fix-free code; prior work solved only the binary three-length case.
method: It introduces a matrix approach based on an exact overlap identity, uses natural numerical order to fix the shortest layer, and applies a fixed-cardinality interpolation theorem with reverse-order selection for uniform cases.

title: Descriptive Complexity In Lean: Completeness By First-Order Reductions
authors: Anton Gnatenko Pierre Senellart
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that descriptive complexity can serve as a foundation for formalizing computational complexity results in a proof assistant, by constructing a Lean library centered around the following concepts: decision problems are isomorphism-invariant predicates on finite structures; complexity classes are defined by their logical characterization; membership is shown by definability witnesses; hardness is shown by first-order reductions from a known hard problem. We also establish bridges to traditional machine models such as (non)deterministic Turing machines. The library proves 73 completeness results, on 68 problems or problem families, over 14 different classes; relations between the classes established inside the logic and not by machine simulation, among them NL = coNL and the Abiteboul-Vianu theorem; and unconditional lower bounds, among them [MATH] and the failure of order-free FO(IFP) to capture PTIME.
tldr: A Lean library formalizing classical descriptive complexity theory, proving 73 completeness results via first-order reductions and logical characterizations of complexity classes.
motivation: The authors aim to show that descriptive complexity can serve as a foundation for mechanically verifying computational complexity results, bridging logical characterizations with traditional machine models.
method: Decision problems are encoded as isomorphism-invariant predicates on finite structures; complexity classes are defined by logical characterizations, membership proven by definability witnesses, and hardness by first-order reductions within the Lean proof assistant.
result: The library establishes 73 completeness results across 68 problems and 14 complexity classes, derives relations such as NL = coNL and the Abiteboul-Vianu theorem internally, and proves unconditional lower bounds including the failure of order-free FO(IFP) to capture PTIME.
conclusion: Descriptive complexity provides a viable formal foundation for machine-checked complexity theory, offering a logical alternative to machine-simulation-based arguments.

title: Brownian Motion With Geometry-dependent Hydrodynamic Memory
authors: Benjamin Sorkin, G\"unther Turk, Howard A. Stone
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Micron-sized particles moving through a fluid are subject to viscous resistance and thermal fluctuations. Beyond steady Stokes friction, colloids also exhibit hydrodynamic memory effects arising from conservation laws of the surrounding fluid. Although fluid-flow problems in complex geometries and confinements are often highly involved, numerical or approximate solutions can be obtained; translating these solutions into closed-form equations of motion for individual colloids, however, is rarely possible. Here, we develop a theoretical framework that provides both underdamped and overdamped colloidal dynamics from the solution of an arbitrary flow problem: (i) Using the Lorentz reciprocal theorem, we express the colloidal equation of motion in terms of the geometry's Green's function and the fluid-flow profile. This formulation yields both the corresponding Stokes drag as well as a Basset-like hydrodynamic memory contribution. (ii) As colloid inertia is often negligible, we furthermore derive the corresponding overdamped (colloid-inertia-less) limit, which inherits the Stokes and Basset-like resistances and additionally gives rise to a spurious drift. We propose applications of this framework to passive and active particles subject to involved confinements and problem geometries.
tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework relating colloidal Brownian motion in arbitrary confined geometries to the fluid's Green's function, yielding Stokes drag plus Basset-like hydrodynamic memory terms in both underdamped and overdamped regimes.
motivation: Micron-scale colloids in fluids exhibit hydrodynamic memory from fluid conservation laws, but translating numerical or approximate flow solutions in complex geometries into closed-form equations of motion for individual particles is rarely possible.
method: Using the Lorentz reciprocal theorem, the authors express the colloidal equation of motion in terms of the geometry's Green's function and the flow profile, obtaining Stokes drag and a Basset-like memory kernel, then take the overdamped (inertia-less) limit.
result: The framework recovers Stokes and Basset-like resistances and reveals an additional spurious drift term in the overdamped limit, with proposed applications to passive and active particles in involved confinements.
conclusion: The formulation provides a general route from arbitrary confined-flow solutions to closed-form colloidal equations of motion, extending classical Brownian dynamics to geometry-dependent hydrodynamic memory.

title: The Fourier Uncertainty Principle Through The Lens Of Infinite Banded Matrices
authors: Cameron L. Williams, Lara C. Ortelli, Gael Silva
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the Fourier uncertainty principle through infinite banded matrices by way of a variational approach to minimizing the uncertainty product. Traditional methods for analyzing the Fourier uncertainty principle rely heavily on the Heisenberg--Weyl structure that underlie the Fourier transform and therefore do not generalize well beyond this setting. We provide three distinct approaches to developing the uncertainty principle based on the spectrum of a shifted quantum harmonic oscillator Hamiltonian, [MATH]. In the Hermite--Gauss basis, [MATH] has an infinite, tridiagonal form which is central to the analysis. One approach exactly solves for the spectrum through analytic methods, another decomposes [MATH] into an infinite sum of [MATH] matrices, and the third approach is an algebraic approach to establishing the spectrum via a unitary equivalence with the quantum harmonic oscillator. The approaches taken herein provide alternate avenues that are more broadly applicable to other canonically conjugate operators for other integral transforms which maintain a tridiagonal form.
tldr: The paper investigates the Fourier uncertainty principle through the spectral analysis of infinite banded matrices derived from a shifted quantum harmonic oscillator Hamiltonian.
motivation: Traditional derivations of the Fourier uncertainty principle rely on the Heisenberg-Weyl structure and do not easily generalize to other canonically conjugate operators or integral transforms.
method: Using the Hermite-Gauss basis, the authors obtain a tridiagonal matrix representation and provide three approaches: analytic spectrum solving, decomposition into an infinite sum of matrices, and algebraic unitary equivalence with the quantum harmonic oscillator.
result: The paper shows that the uncertainty principle can be established from the spectrum of the shifted harmonic oscillator Hamiltonian, yielding alternative derivations that are broadly applicable to other tridiagonal-form operators.
conclusion: These approaches offer new mathematical avenues for uncertainty principles beyond the standard Fourier setting, potentially extending to other integral transforms.

title: Sublattice-selective Control Of Spin Reversal In Metasurface-coupled Kagome Interfaces
authors: Ximo Wang, Qiwei Han, Zhenqi Bai, Ruyue Guo, Min Feng, Yichi Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coherent manipulation of photonic interface states requires a control field that matches their internal mode structure. We study this requirement in a two-component Kagome lattice motivated by photon-mediated exchange near a nonlinear nonlocal metasurface. The Dirac spinors show why uniform Raman control cannot couple opposite-spin, same-valley interface modes at leading order, even when their spatial envelopes coincide. A [MATH] sublattice pattern removes this cancellation and maximizes the projected coupling at fixed root-mean-square amplitude within the diagonal-control class. We test this control scheme through full-zone topology and complete lattice propagation. For a smooth, gapped interface, a [MATH]-dimensional calculation gives target-mode fidelity [MATH] with leakage [MATH] at RMS drive [MATH]. Trace-preserving dynamics gives the separate survival condition needed for successful conversion. An exploratory three-dimensional lithium-niobate supercell reproduces the complex addressing pattern with [MATH] relative error and provides nonlocal exchange, decay and electro-optic frequency-conversion matrices. The mode-resolved control principle thus gives quantitative electromagnetic design targets; the full spin-dependent device realization still requires further calibration.
tldr: The paper analyzes sublattice-selective Raman control for spin reversal in metasurface-coupled Kagome lattice interface states to achieve mode-matched coupling and high-fidelity conversion.
motivation: Coherent manipulation of photonic interface states requires a control field that matches their internal mode structure, but uniform Raman control cannot couple opposite-spin, same-valley interface modes at leading order.
method: The authors use Dirac spinor analysis, full-zone topology, complete lattice propagation simulations, and a three-dimensional lithium-niobate supercell to design and test a sublattice control pattern.
result: A sublattice pattern removes the leading-order cancellation and maximizes projected coupling, yielding target-mode fidelity with low leakage at finite RMS drive; the 3D supercell reproduces the addressing pattern with small relative error.
conclusion: The mode-resolved control principle provides quantitative electromagnetic design targets, but full spin-dependent device realization still requires further calibration.

title: Adaptive Record Consistency In A Schulman-Type Model
authors: D. M. Theshan N. Weerasinghe
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adaptive measurements test whether a retrocausal model preserves observable records when experiments are connected by classical feedback. We establish exact and quantitative composition constraints for a finite-width, coplanar Schulman-type source with positive wrapped-Cauchy propagation weights. Raw segment composition admits an explicit adaptive signalling witness. A uniquely determined scalar correction preserves recorded continuations, and a detector with preparation memory implements this correction while retaining the source correlations. For common, independently prepared terminal detectors coupled to the source through arrival angles, exact calibration forces equal-mass antipodal atomic responses. Under setting-only raw feedback, the sharp minimum worst disturbance of an earlier record is [MATH], where [MATH] is the total source-path width. We derive explicit finite-error bounds and prove linear small-error improvement. For four settings at [MATH], a uniform reduction over arbitrary nonnegative response measures and a continuous polynomial certificate establish [MATH], with [MATH]. A positive five-atom detector attains this coefficient. The results quantify the compatibility of isolated-source accuracy and adaptive record preservation, and provide precise design conditions for retrocausal apparatus models with explicit preparation, memory, and control.
tldr: The paper studies adaptive record consistency in a Schulman-type retrocausal model, deriving composition constraints and signalling witnesses for adaptive measurements with classical feedback.
motivation: To test whether a retrocausal model can preserve observable records when experiments are connected by classical feedback and adaptive measurements.
method: It analyzes a finite-width coplanar Schulman-type source with positive wrapped-Cauchy propagation weights, introduces a uniquely determined scalar correction and a preparation-memory detector, and derives exact finite-error bounds and continuous polynomial certificates for four settings.
result: It finds an explicit adaptive signalling witness for raw segment composition, a scalar correction that preserves recorded continuations, exact calibration forcing equal-mass antipodal atomic responses, and a sharp minimum worst disturbance scaling with the total source-path width; a positive five-atom detector attains the optimal coefficient.
conclusion: The work quantifies the compatibility of isolated-source accuracy and adaptive record preservation, providing precise design conditions for retrocausal apparatus models with explicit preparation, memory, and control.

title: Silicon Avalanche Transition Edge Bolometer: Approaching The Thermodynamic Limit For Uncooled Long-wave Infrared Detection
authors: Wenjun Deng, Renwen Yu, Guanyu Han, Ziyao Feng, Yu Wang, Shanhui Fan, Qiushi Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bolometers transduce incident electromagnetic radiation into measurable electrical signals via radiation-induced heating in thermo-resistive materials. They are uniquely capable of detecting low-energy photons without cryogenic cooling, and are widely deployed for uncooled long-wave infrared (LWIR) radiation detection and thermal imaging. Although their fundamental detection limit is set by the thermodynamic fluctuations, state-of-the-art uncooled bolometers still operate well above this limit due to the presence of Johnson noise, 1/f noise and noises from the readout circuits. Here, we address this challenge by introducing a new uncooled LWIR bolometer concept---the silicon avalanche transition edge (SATE) bolometer. Operating near the steep current transition edge associated with avalanche breakdown, the device exhibits an ultra-high, positive temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR) of 330 %/K, greatly suppressing the impacts of other noise sources. Even without any thermal insulation structures, the SATE bolometer delivers a high room-temperature responsivity up to 160 mA/W for 9.5 [MATH]m radiation, a noise equivalent power of 370 pW/[MATH], and a strong electro-thermal feedback enlarged bandwidth of 77 kHz---performance unattainable with conventional bolometer materials with a TCR of [MATH]/K. Our work establishes a promising thermo-electric transduction mechanism toward high-sensitivity, high-speed room-temperature thermal imaging and infrared spectroscopy using CMOS technology.
tldr: The paper introduces a silicon avalanche transition edge (SATE) bolometer that exploits the steep current transition edge of avalanche breakdown to achieve an ultra-high positive TCR of 330 %/K, enabling uncooled long-wave infrared detection with high responsivity and bandwidth.
motivation: State-of-the-art uncooled bolometers operate far above the fundamental thermodynamic noise limit because of Johnson noise, 1/f noise, and readout noise; a transduction mechanism with a much larger temperature coefficient of resistance could suppress these competing noise sources.
method: The authors design a CMOS-compatible silicon device biased near the avalanche breakdown transition edge, where the current depends extremely steeply on temperature, and characterize its responsivity, noise equivalent power, and electro-thermal feedback bandwidth at room temperature under 9.5 µm illumination.
result: The SATE bolometer achieves 330 %/K TCR, 160 mA/W responsivity at 9.5 µm, NEP of 370 pW/√Hz, and a 77 kHz bandwidth without any thermal insulation structure, surpassing conventional bolometer materials with TCR of ~%/K.
conclusion: The avalanche transition-edge transduction mechanism offers a promising route toward high-sensitivity, high-speed, room-temperature LWIR thermal imaging and infrared spectroscopy using standard CMOS technology.

title: Environmental Qualification And Performance Of A CubeSat-scale Dual Optical Frequency Comb Payload For Space Applications
authors: Stephanie D. Leifer, Matthew J. Kelley, Natalie Walsh, Ziba Shahriary, Paul Steinvurzel, Chrissy Fortuna, Geoffrey Maul, Adam Darley, Ian Coddington, Laura C. Sinclair, Ariel Berman, Victor Chin, Henry Timmers, Kevin Knabe, Jason Pinon, Andrew Attar, Cole Smith, Cyrus Bry, Davis S. Kun, Stan Stanev, Nicole Thai, Bennett Sodergren, Daniel Deveraux, Grant Capan, Will Mcintyre, Manas Choure
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17976v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the environmental qualification and performance of CombSat, a dual optical frequency comb payload designed for deployment on a 12U CubeSat in low Earth orbit. The payload integrates two self-referenced, 200 MHz hybrid fiber-waveguide frequency combs, a narrow-linewidth optical reference, a heterodyne beat detection unit, and FPGA-based control electronics in a total mass of 8.3 kg and volume of 5.7 L, and nominal power consumption of 21W. We describe the mechanical, thermal, and radiation-tolerant design features of the system and present the results of random vibration, storage temperature cycling, and thermal-vacuum testing conducted in accordance with NASA's General Environmental Verification Standard. We show that key comb performance metrics including oscillator and amplifier output power, frep, fCEO, and fopt signal-to-noise ratios, and integrated phase noise, remain within specification after environmental exposure, and we discuss observed failure modes and design modifications that improved robustness. These results demonstrate that compact, low power, fully stabilized, autonomous dual-comb systems can be engineered and qualified for spaceflight on CubeSat platforms, providing a path forward for future low-cost comb-based space applications.
tldr: Reports environmental qualification and performance of a CubeSat-scale dual optical frequency comb payload for space applications.
motivation: Compact, low-power, fully stabilized dual-comb systems could enable low-cost space-based applications such as precision metrology and optical communications.
method: The 12U CubeSat payload integrates two self-referenced 200 MHz hybrid fiber-waveguide combs, a narrow-linewidth optical reference, heterodyne beat detection, and FPGA control, and is subjected to NASA GEVS random vibration, thermal cycling, and thermal-vacuum testing.
result: Key metrics including output power, frep, fCEO, fopt SNR, and integrated phase noise remained within specification after environmental exposure, with observed failure modes informing design improvements.
conclusion: The qualified payload demonstrates that autonomous dual-comb systems can survive spaceflight conditions, providing a path toward future low-cost comb-based space missions.

title: Common Randomness: A Key Enabler Of Trustworthy 6g Communication Systems
authors: Rami Ezzine, Moritz Wiese, Wafa Labidi, Christian Deppe, Holger Boche
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Common randomness (CR) is a valuable resource for enhancing the trustworthiness of 6G communication systems. This article highlights the role of CR in improving scalability, security, and resilience in distributed 6G architectures. It provides an overview of information-theoretic two-source models for CR generation and summarizes known capacity results, together with their implications for practical systems under different communication settings, including one-way, two-way, helper-assisted, and interactive scenarios. Furthermore, the article explores CR-assisted secure identification over Gaussian channels as an application and highlights selected open research problems in CR generation for next-generation wireless systems. The article targets researchers and practitioners interested in bridging information-theoretic tools with emerging 6G communication systems.
tldr: This article overviews common randomness (CR) as a resource for trustworthy 6G communication systems, covering information-theoretic generation models, capacity results, and CR-assisted secure identification over Gaussian channels.
motivation: 6G distributed architectures require improved scalability, security, and resilience, and common randomness is proposed as a valuable resource to achieve these trustworthiness goals.
method: The article reviews information-theoretic two-source models for CR generation, summarizes known capacity results for one-way, two-way, helper-assisted, and interactive communication settings, and explores CR-assisted secure identification over Gaussian channels.
result: It consolidates known capacity results and their practical implications, and identifies selected open research problems in CR generation for next-generation wireless systems.
conclusion: Common randomness is presented as a key enabler for trustworthy 6G, bridging information-theoretic tools with emerging communication applications.

title: Composability Rather Than Computation Sets The Cost Of An Analog Eml Hardware Fabric
authors: C. Teuscher
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The operator eml(x, y) = exp(x) - ln(y) with the constant 1 generates the elementary functions, a continuous counterpart to NAND. Whether it yields a useful fabric had not been asked of hardware. We ask in network models, circuit simulation and SkyWater 130 nm layout. Four bipolar junctions evaluate the operator for 13 fJ, beating a width-matched digital datapath by 4-134x. The fabric assembled from them is not cheap: it loses to resource-matched baselines, and over the reals its grammar excludes trigonometry. Amplifiers holding those junctions' operating points take 74.5% of a cell's current, so a cell costs 3000 times what they spend. Extracted non-idealities cost 2.6x when a cell must hold a value and nothing when it need only be repeatable. Sharing them across cells recovers two of the three orders. The premise was that a universal primitive licenses a uniform machine. It survives in the primitive and fails in the machine.
tldr: The paper evaluates an analog hardware fabric based on the universal elementary-function operator eml(x,y)=exp(x)-ln(y) and finds that composability, not computational universality, dominates its cost.
motivation: The operator eml with constant 1 is a continuous counterpart to NAND and could in principle provide a universal primitive for analog computation, but whether it enables a useful hardware fabric had not been studied.
method: The author uses network models, circuit simulation, and a SkyWater 130 nm layout to assess bipolar-junction implementations of eml and compare them against width-matched digital datapaths and resource-matched baselines.
result: Four bipolar junctions evaluate the operator for 13 fJ, beating a digital datapath by 4–134x, but the assembled fabric loses to resource-matched baselines; amplifiers holding operating points consume 74.5% of cell current, making cells 3000x more expensive, and extracted non-idealities cost 2.6x when holding values.
conclusion: The premise that a universal primitive licenses a uniform machine fails in practice: it survives at the primitive level but not at the machine level because composability overheads dominate cost.

title: An Operator Approach To Register Programs For Catalytic Computing
authors: Antoine Vinciguerra
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a seminal work, Buhrman et al.\ (STOC 2014) introduced catalytic computation and proved that uniform [MATH] circuits are computable in catalytic logspace, the class of problems solvable in space [MATH] with an additional catalytic tape of size [MATH], a tape whose initial content must be restored at the end of the computation. A central ingredient of their proof is the register program model. Namely, they constructed a uniform family of register programs that computes [MATH] using [MATH] registers and four accesses to [MATH]. Since then, determining the number of registers and input accesses required to compute a polynomial of a given degree has become a central question in the study of catalytic computation. On one hand, we prove that the four-access bound of Buhrman et al.\ is optimal: every passive-output register program computing a polynomial of degree greater than three requires at least four input accesses, independently of the number of registers. On the other hand, we show that their register bound is not optimal. For every [MATH] and every field [MATH] of characteristic [MATH] or greater than [MATH], we construct a register program for [MATH] with four input accesses and [MATH] registers. Our proofs rely on derivations and their exponential operators. This approach represents a register program as a series of exponential derivation operators, reducing register restoration to an operator identity. Finally, we use the uniform family of register programs to improve known trade-offs for catalytic streaming algorithms and register programs for matrix powering. The generalization of the lower-bound methods and the construction of the uniform family of register programs were developed with assistance from ChatGPT 5.6.
tldr: The paper studies register program models for catalytic computation, proving the optimality of the four-input-access bound and constructing improved register programs for polynomial evaluation.
motivation: Since Buhrman et al. introduced catalytic computation and the register program model, determining the minimum number of registers and input accesses needed to compute polynomials of a given degree has become a central open question.
method: The authors represent register programs as sequences of exponential derivation operators, reducing the register restoration requirement to an operator identity, and use this to derive both lower and upper bounds.
result: They show that four input accesses are necessary for any passive-output register program computing a polynomial of degree greater than three, and construct register programs with four accesses using O(log^2 n) registers, improving trade-offs for catalytic streaming and matrix powering.
conclusion: The operator-theoretic framework tightens bounds in catalytic computing and yields a uniform family of register programs, though the topic is a purely classical complexity result with no quantum information, thermodynamic, network, or hybrid-platform component.

title: QiT: Quantum-Inspired Transformer For Visual Recognition Task
authors: Vijay Agneeswaran Badri N. Patro
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17789v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum machine learning offers a compelling representational perspective: angle-encoded states inhabit Hilbert spaces in which periodic similarities and interactions can be expressed naturally. Realizing this perspective for visual recognition remains difficult, however, because present quantum neural networks are constrained by limited qubit counts, costly circuit simulation and measurement, noise, and unstable optimization on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. We investigate whether useful structural ideas from quantum models can instead be realized as scalable classical Transformer operations. We introduce QiT, a Quantum-inspired Transformer for vision tasks with three components: (i) angle-inspired encoding that maps image tokens to learned trigonometric Hilbert-space features analogous to quantum rotation-based state encoding; (ii) self-attention over these periodic features, inducing a classical cosine kernel approximated to quantum fidelity kernels; and (iii) gated multiplicative emulation, a trainable classical surrogate for interaction terms found in variational circuits. All components are differentiable tensor operations, so QiT claims neither quantum computation nor quantum speedup and retains the [MATH] attention complexity of a standard Vision Transformer. Across image-classification benchmarks, QiT is competitive with a matched classical Transformer while avoiding the severe runtime cost observed for a small simulated quantum Transformer. QiT-B reaches 78.3\% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 45.7M parameters and 11.5 GFLOPs. These results position QiT as a scalable baseline for isolating and evaluating quantum-motivated inductive biases in visual recognition.
tldr: QiT is a classical Vision Transformer whose token encodings, attention kernels, and interaction terms are designed to mimic angle-encoded quantum states, but it performs no quantum computation and claims no quantum advantage.
motivation: Quantum machine learning offers appealing representations via angle-encoded states in Hilbert space, but current quantum neural networks are limited by qubit counts, noisy simulation, and unstable optimization, so the authors ask whether quantum-motivated structural ideas can be captured in scalable classical Transformers.
method: The model uses angle-inspired trigonometric feature encoding of image tokens, self-attention as a classical cosine kernel approximating quantum fidelity kernels, and gated multiplicative emulation of variational-circuit interaction terms, all as differentiable tensor operations with standard ViT attention complexity.
