result: QiT-B reaches 78.3% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 45.7M parameters and 11.5 GFLOPs, matching a comparable classical Transformer while avoiding the runtime cost of a small simulated quantum Transformer.
conclusion: The work positions QiT as a scalable classical baseline for isolating quantum-motivated inductive biases in visual recognition, without claiming quantum computation or speedup.

title: Macroscopic Response Diagnoses The Noise Sensitivity Of Terminal Outcomes
authors: Chaoqian Wang Bo Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can the terminal macroscopic outcome of a many-body system be inferred from its microscopic initial data without simulating the full trajectory? Rather than construct such a shortcut, we address a more fundamental question for Gaussian microscopic inputs: can any fixed Wiener-Hermite degree retain a nonvanishing fraction of the variance of the terminal outcome as the system grows? We consider homogeneous systems with independent Gaussian disorder in which all microscopic coordinates are symmetry-equivalent, the terminal event is monotone in each disorder variable, and a uniform disorder shift is exactly equivalent to a control-field shift with a size-independent conversion factor. Using forward and inverse Gaussian influence bounds together with a Gaussian Russo formula, we derive a directly measurable criterion that is both necessary and sufficient for noise sensitivity. Specifically, the correlation between the original and coordinate-perturbed terminal outcomes vanishes asymptotically for every fixed nonzero level of coordinatewise noise if and only if the slope of the outcome probability with respect to the control field at the balanced threshold grows more slowly than the square root of the system volume. Event-driven simulations of the three-dimensional driven random-field Ising model up to linear size 192 find that both the normalized response and the correlations between perturbed samples decrease overall, consistent with the noise-sensitive regime at finite size. For spatial Stag-Hunt dynamics with prescribed seeds, the criterion generalizes through an effective number of influential coordinates. Separately, simulations of a path-dependent best-response game show, over the sizes studied, that the terminal equilibrium can depend on the update schedule while still carrying substantial finite-order predictive information.
tldr: The paper derives a measurable criterion for when terminal macroscopic outcomes in disordered many-body systems become noise-sensitive, using Gaussian influence bounds and simulations of driven random-field Ising and game dynamics.
motivation: The authors ask whether the terminal macroscopic outcome of a many-body system can be inferred from microscopic initial data without full simulation, and more fundamentally whether any fixed Wiener-Hermite degree retains predictive variance as system size grows.
method: For homogeneous systems with independent Gaussian disorder, monotone terminal events, and a uniform disorder shift equivalent to a control-field shift, they combine forward and inverse Gaussian influence bounds with a Gaussian Russo formula to derive a necessary and sufficient criterion for noise sensitivity.
result: The criterion states that correlations between original and coordinate-perturbed terminal outcomes vanish asymptotically for any fixed nonzero coordinatewise noise iff the slope of outcome probability with respect to the control field at the balanced threshold grows slower than the square root of the system volume; simulations of 3D driven random-field Ising model up to size 192 and Stag-Hunt dynamics support the noise-sensitive regime at finite size.
conclusion: Macroscopic response can diagnose noise sensitivity in these systems, and a path-dependent best-response game shows terminal equilibrium can depend on update schedule while retaining finite-order predictive information.

title: Improved Lattice Boltzmann Method For Conjugate Magnetohydrodynamic Simulations
authors: Jun Li, Wai Hong Ronald Chan, Kun Ting Eddie Chua
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the simulation of conjugate magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) flows, where a moving conducting fluid dynamically interacts with bounding conducting walls under the influence of an externally imposed magnetic field, resolving the electrical conductivity transition across the fluid-solid interface introduces significant numerical challenges. In problems with high magnetic Reynolds numbers, it is required to solve the full magnetic induction formulation that has a curl-of-curl term for the magnetic diffusion, which is simplified to a divergence term in the original vector-valued lattice Boltzmann method (LBM). The resulting LBM scheme is valid for simulating fluid domains with a constant conductivity where its bounding solid walls are modelled using appropriate boundary conditions. The current study shows that this scheme is also valid for two-dimensional conjugate MHD simulations where the magnetic field component with non-zero gradients is perpendicular to the conductivity gradient. For general conjugate MHD simulations, we improve the LBM scheme by considering the difference between the curl-of-curl term and the simplified divergence form, which is treated as a source term in the LBM evolution algorithm and computed using an efficient LBM discretisation scheme. The improved LBM scheme automatically satisfies the required conjugate constraints at the fluid-solid interface as a volume integral inside two adjacent boundary layers. The accuracy of the improved LBM scheme is verified by piecewise analytical solutions in benchmark problems with an abrupt conductivity jump across the fluid-solid interface.
tldr: The paper improves a vector-valued lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) to handle conjugate magnetohydrodynamic flows with abrupt electrical conductivity jumps across fluid-solid interfaces.
motivation: Conjugate MHD simulations, where conducting fluids interact with conducting walls, are numerically challenging because the electrical conductivity discontinuity at the interface and the full curl-of-curl magnetic diffusion term are difficult to resolve accurately.
method: The authors show the existing LBM scheme is valid only when the magnetic field gradient direction is perpendicular to the conductivity gradient, and generalize it by treating the difference between the curl-of-curl term and its simplified divergence form as a source term, discretized efficiently within the LBM evolution and enforced as a volume integral across adjacent boundary layers.
result: The improved scheme automatically satisfies the conjugate interface constraints and is validated against piecewise analytical benchmark solutions with an abrupt conductivity jump at the fluid-solid interface.
conclusion: The improved LBM provides an accurate and general numerical framework for two- and three-dimensional conjugate MHD simulations, extending the applicability of vector-valued lattice Boltzmann methods to general conductivity gradients.

title: Non-homogeneous Partial Differential Wave Equation For The Description Of Correlated Pair States In The Microworld
authors: Alireza Khalili Golmankhaneh Elmira Isayeva
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, a new non-homogeneous linear second-order partial differential equation (PDE) is proposed and investigated, designed to describe the dynamics of correlated pair objects of the microworld (analogues of Cooper pairs or biphotons). The fundamental complex solution of the proposed equation initially contains a spatial background and a doubled phase, which allows for a natural localization of the pair condensate in space. In this work, the continuity and energy balance equations are derived, the discrete spectrum in potential fields is calculated, and specific effects of tunneling and nonlinear interaction of the pair conglomerate with electromagnetic radiation are described.
tldr: The paper proposes a new non-homogeneous linear second-order PDE to model correlated pair objects (Cooper-pair or biphoton analogues) of the microworld.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a unified wave-equation framework for describing the dynamics of correlated pair states in the microscopic domain.
method: A non-homogeneous linear PDE is introduced whose complex solution carries a spatial background and doubled phase; continuity and energy balance equations are derived, discrete spectra in potential fields computed, and tunneling plus nonlinear interaction with electromagnetic radiation are analyzed.
result: The solution naturally localizes a pair condensate in space, yields discrete spectra for confining potentials, and describes tunneling and nonlinear pair–radiation interaction effects.
conclusion: The proposed PDE offers a formal phenomenological description of correlated pair states, though it is not connected to quantum information, thermodynamic, networking, or hybrid-platform research.

title: Centroids For Weak Optimal Transport With Barycentric Cost
authors: Friedemann Krannich
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We generalize the theory of Wasserstein barycenters between N given measures from the Wasserstein distance to the weak optimal transport problem with barycentric cost. We find a multi-marginal formulation and its dual problem. The multi-marginal problem is new in itself; contrary to the classical multi-marginal optimal transport problem, the first M marginals of its competitors are not fixed but instead only need dominate the first M given measures in convex order, while the last N-M marginals of its competitors are dominated in convex order by the last N-M given measures.
tldr: The paper generalizes Wasserstein barycenters to weak optimal transport with barycentric cost, providing a multi-marginal formulation and its dual.
motivation: Wasserstein barycenters are central in optimal transport, but their extension to weak optimal transport with barycentric cost had not been systematically developed.
method: The author introduces a multi-marginal optimal transport problem whose first M marginals only need to dominate given measures in convex order, while the last N-M marginals are dominated in convex order, and derives its dual problem.
result: A new multi-marginal formulation and dual problem are obtained for weak optimal transport barycenters, distinct from the classical fixed-marginal multi-marginal transport problem.
conclusion: This work advances the mathematical theory of barycenters in weak optimal transport, with potential applications in areas where only convex-order constraints are natural.

title: Entropy And Translation Length In The Ray Graph
authors: Juliette Bavard, Danny Calegari, Alden Walker
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be the mapping class group of the plane minus a Cantor set, acting on the ray graph [MATH], and for [MATH] let [MATH] denote the translation length of [MATH] on [MATH]. We prove that [MATH] for every [MATH] diffeomorphism [MATH] of [MATH] representing [MATH], where [MATH] denotes topological entropy. The proof falls into two parts: a combinatorial argument bounding distance between two rays in [MATH] by the logarithm of the geometric intersection number; and a geometric argument that promotes geometric control (coarse length of iterates of a fixed ray) to combinatorial control (geometric intersection number). motivation: The ray graph is a hyperbolic complex on which the mapping class group of the plane minus a Cantor set acts, and relating dynamical invariants such as topological entropy to combinatorial translation lengths illuminates the geometry of this action.
method: The proof combines a combinatorial argument bounding the distance between two rays by the logarithm of the geometric intersection number with a geometric argument promoting coarse control of iterates of a fixed ray to combinatorial control.
result: The authors establish the inequality relating translation length and topological entropy for all diffeomorphisms representing a given mapping class, and conjecture that an additional hypothesis in their theorem can be removed.
conclusion: The work connects topological dynamics to the coarse geometry of the ray graph, leaving an open conjecture about strengthening the bound.

title: Prediction With Five Experts And Geometric Stopping: A Probabilistic Construction And Analytic Verification
authors: Erhan Bayraktar, Ibrahim Ekren, Nikolaos Kolliopoulos
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a solution of the limiting five-expert prediction problem with geometric stopping, based on stochastic calculus and partial differential equations. If [MATH] is the stopping probability, the minimax expected regret from tied initial scores is [MATH] as [MATH]. The adversarial rank control selecting the best and third-best experts maximizes the limiting Hamiltonian at every state. Following the four-expert construction of Bayraktar, Ekren, and Zhang (2020), we represent the value correction as a discounted boundary-local-time expectation for a degenerate obliquely reflected Brownian motion. The hyperbolic systems governing its boundary traces are derived and solved explicitly. To verify the nonlinear Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation, we combine equality directions, hyperbolic comparison principles, and averaging across controls. These arguments reduce the 48 regional control inequalities to lower-dimensional boundary problems, with the remaining signs established by explicit monotonicity arguments. We prove global [MATH] regularity across both regional interfaces and changes in rank ordering. We also show that the alternating COMB control attains the limiting Hamiltonian maximum exactly when the two highest scores coincide and the third- and fourth-highest scores coincide.
tldr: The paper solves a limiting five-expert prediction problem with geometric stopping using stochastic calculus, PDEs, and Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman verification.
motivation: The problem extends prediction with expert advice to a minimax setting with adversarial rank control and geometric stopping, aiming to characterize optimal regret and value corrections.
method: The authors construct the value correction via a discounted boundary-local-time expectation for a degenerate obliquely reflected Brownian motion, derive and solve hyperbolic systems for boundary traces, and verify the nonlinear HJB equation using equality directions, hyperbolic comparison principles, and averaging across controls.
result: They prove global regularity across regional interfaces and rank-ordering changes, reduce 48 regional control inequalities to lower-dimensional boundary problems, and show the alternating COMB control attains the limiting Hamiltonian maximum exactly in a specific score-coincidence case.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous analytic solution to the five-expert geometric stopping problem and verifies the associated HJB equation, advancing stochastic control and prediction theory rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Computing Stationary Equilibria In Measure-Dependent Markov Systems
authors: Jing Dong, Bar Light, Xin Tong
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many stochastic systems in operations and economics exhibit feedback between their long-run state distribution and the transition law governing their dynamics. In this paper, we develop a computational framework for stationary equilibria in such measure-dependent Markov systems when this feedback operates through a finite-dimensional aggregate. We show that the original stationary-equilibrium problem can be reduced to a finite-dimensional self-consistency equation, separating steady-state analysis of the underlying Markov system from equilibrium computation. We use properties of the resulting self-consistency map to guide the choice among fixed-point iteration, relaxed fixed-point iteration, and minimization of the fixed-point residual. The last approach requires derivatives of the self-consistency map, which are typically unavailable in closed form. We therefore develop finite-time infinitesimal perturbation analysis estimators for these derivatives, with error bounds that separate Monte Carlo error from finite-time bias. We illustrate the framework through a strategic [MATH] queue and an opinion-dynamics model, showing how different structural properties lead naturally to different equilibrium-computation methods.
tldr: The paper develops a computational framework for finding stationary equilibria in measure-dependent Markov systems where the transition law depends on the long-run state distribution through a finite-dimensional aggregate.
motivation: Many stochastic systems in operations research and economics exhibit feedback between their steady-state distribution and their own dynamics, but computing such equilibria is difficult because the fixed-point map generally lacks closed-form structure.
method: The authors reduce the stationary-equilibrium problem to a finite-dimensional self-consistency equation and compare fixed-point iteration, relaxed fixed-point iteration, and residual minimization; they also derive finite-time infinitesimal perturbation analysis estimators for the required derivatives with Monte Carlo error and finite-time bias bounds.
result: The framework is illustrated on a strategic queueing model and an opinion-dynamics model, showing how structural properties of each system naturally suggest different equilibrium-computation methods.
conclusion: The work provides a general and practically guided computational toolkit for measure-dependent Markov equilibria, but it is entirely classical in nature and has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Improved Lower Bounds For Decomposable Randomized Encoding
authors: Kewen Wu Justin Holmgren
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A decomposable randomized encoding (DRE) for a function [MATH] allows [MATH] parties, using shared randomness, to encode their individual inputs locally so that the collection of encodings reveals [MATH] and nothing else. DREs are widely used in efficient multiparty computation. Their main complexity measure is size, the total bit length of the local encodings. Yet the optimal DRE size remains poorly understood even for the [MATH]-bit OR function. We prove the first superlinear lower bound for OR and, more generally, for every non-periodic symmetric function. Under an additional symmetry assumption, we prove a sharp [MATH] lower bound for OR, matching the classic construction of Feige, Kilian, and Naor (STOC 1994). We also prove the first [MATH] lower bound on DRE size for non-explicit Boolean functions.
tldr: The paper proves the first superlinear lower bounds on the size of decomposable randomized encodings (DREs) for the OR function and other non-periodic symmetric functions, plus the first superpolynomial lower bound for non-explicit Boolean functions.
motivation: DREs are fundamental building blocks for efficient secure multiparty computation, yet the optimal DRE size is poorly understood even for simple functions like OR.
method: The authors use complexity-theoretic techniques to establish lower bounds, including a sharp quadratic (n^2) lower bound for OR under an additional symmetry assumption that matches the classic Feige–Kilian–Naor construction.
result: They obtain the first superlinear lower bound for OR and all non-periodic symmetric functions, a sharp n^2 lower bound matching FKN under symmetry, and a superpolynomial lower bound on DRE size for non-explicit Boolean functions.
conclusion: These results substantially tighten our understanding of the size complexity of randomized encodings, closing gaps between upper and lower bounds for canonical functions used in multiparty cryptography.

title: Hidden Circuits And Exact Counting In Ordered Graphs
authors: Boning Meng Chenghua Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that counting perfect matchings is [MATH]-complete under polynomial-time Turing reductions on each of three classes of simple, unweighted graphs: monotone graphs, unit interval graphs, and chordal permutation graphs. The monotone result settles the exact-counting complexity left open by Dyer, Jerrum, and M\"uller (JACM 2017), complementing their rapid-mixing theorem. Inspired by quantum circuits, our reductions implement a circuit simulation using globally coupled matching-transfer operators. The key construction is an exact projection, implemented by a polynomial-length sequence of normalized transfers, that restores tensor-product locality and makes encoded gates composable. Interpolation-based cancellation then reduces circuit evaluation to unweighted perfect-matching counts in all three classes. We also place Dyer and M\"uller's class QChains within the distance-hereditary graphs and give an [MATH]-arithmetic-operation counting algorithm for the latter, improving the [MATH] bound obtainable from Curticapean and Marx (SODA 2016). Together with prior results, these advances complete the exact-counting classification of the graph classes in Dyer and M\"uller's diagram (SIDMA 2019).
tldr: The paper proves that counting perfect matchings is #P-complete under polynomial-time Turing reductions for monotone graphs, unit interval graphs, and chordal permutation graphs, using circuit-simulation constructions inspired by quantum circuits.
motivation: Dyer, Jerrum, and Müller left the exact-counting complexity of monotone graphs open, and the classification of exact-counting complexity across the graph classes in their diagram was incomplete.
method: The authors build reductions that simulate a circuit using globally coupled matching-transfer operators, with an exact projection implemented via a polynomial-length sequence of normalized transfers to restore tensor-product locality, combined with interpolation-based cancellation.
result: Counting perfect matchings is shown #P-complete for all three graph classes, a #P-arithmetic counting algorithm is given for distance-hereditary graphs (improving on Curticapean–Marx), and QChains is placed within distance-hereditary graphs.
conclusion: The results complete the exact-counting classification of graph classes in Dyer and Müller's diagram, settling a previously open problem.

title: Generalized $p$-ary $\cPS$ Bent Functions
authors: Mohit Pal Alexander Kholosha
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We use [MATH]-dimensional partial spreads of [MATH], where [MATH] is an odd prime, [MATH] is a positive integer and [MATH] divides [MATH], to construct two classes of bent functions from [MATH] to [MATH]. Our construction generalizes the classes of [MATH]-ary [MATH] and [MATH] bent functions proposed by P. Lison\v ek and H. Y. Lu (Des. Codes Cryptogr. 73 (2014), 209--216).
tldr: The paper constructs two new classes of p-ary bent functions from partial spreads in finite fields, generalizing earlier p-ary and 2-ary bent function constructions.
motivation: Bent functions are maximally nonlinear Boolean/vectorial functions with applications in cryptography, coding theory, and sequence design, and known constructions over odd-characteristic fields are limited.
method: Using (p-ary) partial spreads of the finite field geometry, the authors build functions from the field to the base field and prove their bentness by analyzing the associated Walsh–Hadamard spectra.
result: Two new infinite families of p-ary bent functions are obtained, which contain as special cases the p-ary and 2-ary bent function classes of Lisonek and Lu (2014).
conclusion: The construction broadens the set of known p-ary bent functions, providing new cryptographic functions, though the work remains purely within classical finite-field combinatorics and cryptography.

title: Seek: Secure And Efficient Encrypted Keyword Search For Privacy-Preserving Messaging Protocols
authors: Michail Maniatakos Soumyadyuti Ghosh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Encrypted communication protects sensitive user data but can facilitate harmful or unlawful exchanges, creating a trade-off between detecting dangerous messages and preserving end-user privacy. To address this, we propose SEEK, a practical and efficient encrypted keyword-search protocol for privacy-preserving messaging that combines homomorphic encryption with secure two-party computation (2PC). SEEK first partitions messages into ciphertext fragments with the minimum sufficient overlap, then homomorphically correlates them using encrypted keyword trapdoors. For long messages, this design can reduce sender-side encryption and upload overhead by up to two orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art baselines. It supports ASCII case-insensitive matching with one fixed-size encrypted trapdoor and one homomorphic multiplication per fragment, yielding up to 5.47x faster correlation computation than the strongest fragmentation-based baselines. SEEK then invokes 2PC-based selected decoding, blinded zero testing, and secure aggregation, revealing only the keyword presence-or-absence bit while hiding the keyword, its length, message contents, match counts, and locations. SEEK achieves 100% accuracy under case variations that result in exact-matching failures, without requiring additional trapdoors or online communication. We further realize SEEK as an end-to-end web and cross-platform mobile application. Prototype evaluation on a weekly messaging history yields an online computation time of 1.92 s per search, demonstrating the practical feasibility and efficiency of SEEK.
tldr: SEEK is a classical encrypted keyword-search protocol combining homomorphic encryption and secure two-party computation for privacy-preserving messaging.
motivation: Encrypted communication protects privacy but can hinder detection of harmful messages, creating a trade-off between privacy and content moderation.
method: SEEK partitions messages into ciphertext fragments with minimal overlap, performs homomorphic correlation using encrypted keyword trapdoors, and then uses 2PC-based selected decoding, blinded zero testing, and secure aggregation.
result: The protocol reduces sender-side overhead by up to two orders of magnitude, achieves up to 5.47x faster correlation than fragmentation baselines, and runs in 1.92 s per search on a weekly messaging history prototype.
conclusion: SEEK demonstrates practical and efficient encrypted keyword search for messaging applications while hiding keywords, message contents, match counts, and locations.

title: Towards A Proof-Theoretic Analysis Of Incorrect/Incomplete Proofs
authors: Mariami Gamsakhurdia Matthias Baaz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the proof-theoretic structure of incorrect/incomplete proofs, that is, derivations containing syntactic errors or incomplete inferential steps that nonetheless preserve partial semantic validity. Building on Hilbert's epsilon calculus, we formalize how such derivations can be corrected through semantic projection and weakest preconditions, leading to valid Herbrand disjunctions. We show that the epsilon calculus provides a natural framework for analyzing tolerance of falsity in proofs and for identifying conditions under which an incorrect proof can be semantically repaired. This approach extends Hilbert's program beyond correctness, toward a logic of error and recovery. Moreover we show that the extended first epsilon theorem is false-tolerant.
tldr: The paper develops a proof-theoretic framework in Hilbert's epsilon calculus for analyzing and repairing incorrect or incomplete proofs that preserve partial semantic validity.
motivation: The authors aim to extend Hilbert's program beyond correctness by formalizing a logic of error and recovery for derivations containing syntactic errors or incomplete inferential steps.
method: They build on Hilbert's epsilon calculus to formalize correction through semantic projection and weakest preconditions, leading to valid Herbrand disjunctions.
result: They show that the epsilon calculus naturally analyzes tolerance of falsity and conditions under which an incorrect proof can be semantically repaired, and prove that the extended first epsilon theorem is false-tolerant.
conclusion: The work offers a proof-theoretic foundation for reasoning about incorrect proofs and their semantic repair, moving toward a logic of error and recovery.

title: Monodromy Eigenvectors For Difference Equations With Root-of-Unity Step
authors: Alexander Varchenko Vitaly Tarasov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A qKZ-type discrete flat connection with multiplicative step [MATH] has monodromy operators when [MATH] is a root of unity. The monodromy operators are commuting endomorphisms of the connection. We construct their eigensections and eigenvalues. The construction is based on the presentation of the discrete flat connection as a discrete Gauss-Manin connection.
tldr: The paper constructs eigensections and eigenvalues of monodromy operators for a qKZ-type discrete flat connection with multiplicative step at a root of unity.
motivation: Monodromy of qKZ-type connections is central in representation theory and integrable systems, especially at roots of unity where the step size degenerates and new spectral phenomena appear.
method: The authors represent the discrete flat connection as a discrete Gauss-Manin connection and use this geometric presentation to build commuting monodromy operators and explicitly solve their eigenproblem.
result: They obtain explicit eigensections and eigenvalues for the monodromy operators in the root-of-unity case.
conclusion: The work provides a spectral description of monodromy for qKZ-type difference equations and connects it to discrete Gauss-Manin theory, though it remains a pure mathematical contribution outside the specified quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems directions.

title: Hydrodynamic Memory In Overdamped Colloidal Dynamics
authors: Benjamin Sorkin, G\"unther Turk, Howard A. Stone
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Micron-sized colloid particles diffusing through a fluid experience hydrodynamic inertial and memory effects, the latter causing velocity autocorrelation to decay as a power law. At the same time, many theoretical descriptions treat colloidal diffusion in a fluid using overdamped Langevin dynamics for its convenience, eliminating velocity, omitting inertia, but also ignoring the power-law memory. In this Letter, we show that hydrodynamic memory survives in the overdamped (colloid-inertialess) limit. By identifying the dimensionless parameter controlling the crossover between early- and late-time dynamics, we derive in closed form the overdamped Langevin equation in the presence of hydrodynamic memory. This provides a theoretical framework for realistically describing colloidal dynamics in a fluid, and establishes a rigorous basis for the positional memory observed in high-resolution experiments. Our theory predicts that hydrodynamic memory becomes increasingly pronounced for smaller particles and under stronger external forcing, and offers experimental probes for the crossover from conventional exponential relaxation to memory-dominated power-law dynamics.
tldr: Hydrodynamic memory persists in overdamped colloidal dynamics, leading to power-law velocity autocorrelation and positional memory.
motivation: Overdamped Langevin dynamics is widely used for colloidal diffusion but ignores hydrodynamic memory, which causes velocity autocorrelation to decay as a power law. This work aims to incorporate memory effects into the overdamped limit.
method: The authors identify a dimensionless parameter controlling the crossover between early- and late-time dynamics and derive a closed-form overdamped Langevin equation with hydrodynamic memory.
result: The theory predicts that hydrodynamic memory becomes more pronounced for smaller particles and stronger external forcing, and provides experimental probes for the crossover from exponential relaxation to power-law dynamics.
conclusion: This work provides a rigorous framework for describing colloidal dynamics with memory, establishing a basis for positional memory observed in experiments and offering testable predictions.

title: On Imaging Capabilities Of The Imaging And Medical Beamline At The Australian Synchrotron
authors: T. E. Gureyev, K. M. Pavlov, C. J. Hall, A. Maksimenko, D. Pelliccia, D. M. Paganin, A. W. Stevenson, A. Entezam, H. M. Quiney
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several propagation-based and analyser-based X-ray phase-contrast imaging experiments with over 100 m between the imaged objects and the detector were carried out at the Imaging and Medical beamline (IMBL) of the Australian Synchrotron. These experiments were aimed at characterization of possible phase-contrast imaging setups at IMBL. Effects of the beam divergence, polychromaticity and X-ray source size on the contrast and spatial resolution of images were evaluated quantitatively in different imaging scenarios. The results of this work will be used for improving the existing and developing new imaging capabilities at the beamline. Applications to X-ray phase-contrast tomography of biomedical samples, particularly for medical breast cancer imaging, are briefly discussed.
tldr: Propagation-based and analyser-based X-ray phase-contrast imaging experiments with over 100 m propagation distance were performed at the Australian Synchrotron's Imaging and Medical Beamline to characterize imaging setups.
motivation: The beamline aims to characterize and improve its phase-contrast imaging capabilities, particularly for biomedical applications such as breast cancer imaging, where beam divergence, polychromaticity, and source size affect image quality.
method: Long-propagation-distance phase-contrast imaging experiments were conducted at IMBL, with quantitative evaluation of beam divergence, polychromaticity, and X-ray source size effects on image contrast and spatial resolution across different imaging scenarios.
result: The effects of beam divergence, polychromaticity, and source size on contrast and spatial resolution were quantitatively characterized for various phase-contrast imaging configurations.
conclusion: The findings will guide improvements to existing and new imaging capabilities at the beamline and support applications to X-ray phase-contrast tomography of biomedical samples.

title: Bounded Integer Quadratic Programming Through Parallelepiped Covers And Discrete Convic Optimization
authors: Robert Hildebrand Cinar Ari
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an exact algorithm for minimizing an arbitrary rational quadratic polynomial [MATH] over the integer points of a bounded rational polyhedron [MATH]. For [MATH] variables and [MATH] inequalities, the running time is $[MATH][MATH]\beta[MATH]A[MATH]Q[MATH]L[MATH]L[MATH]b[MATH]c[MATH]\gamma$ enters only this fixed-degree factor. Our algorithm refines the integral parallelepiped cover of Goemans and Rothvoss into cells with controlled displacement sets. On each cell, either an integer displacement of negative quadratic value rules out every point as a global minimizer, or the quadratic identity supplies a separation oracle for the convex hull of each integer objective sublevel set. The integer-query feasibility theorem of Hildebrand and Goess then finds the cell minimum. A refinement through scaled lattices solves the displacement search, and a localization argument separates the encoding dependence of the constraint matrix and quadratic part from that of the remaining data. Combining the bounded algorithm with the unboundedness test of Ari and Hildebrand extends the method to arbitrary rational polyhedra.
tldr: This paper presents an exact algorithm for minimizing a rational quadratic polynomial over the integer points of a bounded rational polyhedron using parallelepiped covers and discrete convex optimization techniques.
motivation: Integer quadratic programming is a fundamental problem in combinatorial optimization, and exact algorithms with improved running times are of significant theoretical interest.
method: The authors refine the integral parallelepiped cover of Goemans and Rothvoss into cells with controlled displacement sets, use a quadratic identity to construct separation oracles for sublevel sets, and employ an integer-query feasibility theorem with scaled lattice refinements and localization arguments.
result: The algorithm runs in time polynomial in the input size and the bit sizes of the data, with the dependence on certain parameters confined to a fixed-degree factor, and it extends to arbitrary rational polyhedra via an unboundedness test.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of exact integer quadratic programming but is not related to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Torus Bifurcation In The Hopf-Langford Type System Through Averaging Theory
authors: Gustavo Domingues
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the existence of periodic solutions and invariant tori bifurcating from a zero-Hopf equilibrium in a Hopf-Langford type system. Using second-order averaging theory, we establish explicit parameter conditions under which the system admits a periodic solution near the origin, together with its stability. We then apply recent results relating invariant tori to Neimark-Sacker bifurcations of the associated Poincar\'e map to obtain a smooth bifurcation curve along which a unique invariant torus surrounds the periodic solution. The relevant first Lyapunov coefficient is computed explicitly as a power series in the perturbation parameter, and we show that, under the conditions considered, this coefficient is always positive; consequently, whenever it exists, the bifurcating torus is unstable, regardless of the specific parameter values chosen within our hypotheses. This provides a structural obstruction to the existence of asymptotically stable tori in this family of systems. We illustrate our results with two numerical examples, one exhibiting an isolated asymptotically stable periodic solution with no bifurcating torus, and another exhibiting a periodic solution surrounded by an unstable invariant torus, the latter also illustrated through its Poincar\'e map.
tldr: This paper studies periodic solutions and invariant tori bifurcating from a zero-Hopf equilibrium in a Hopf-Langford type system using second-order averaging theory.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize bifurcations of invariant tori in a specific dynamical system family and to determine conditions for their stability.
method: They apply second-order averaging theory to establish parameter conditions for periodic solutions and use results relating invariant tori to Neimark-Sacker bifurcations of the Poincaré map, computing the first Lyapunov coefficient explicitly.
result: They find that under the studied conditions the first Lyapunov coefficient is always positive, implying that any bifurcating torus is unstable, thus providing a structural obstruction to asymptotically stable tori in this family.
conclusion: The paper provides explicit bifurcation conditions and stability results for invariant tori in the Hopf-Langford type system, illustrated by two numerical examples.

title: Pinching-Antenna-Enabled Isac: A Unified Architecture For Flexible Communication And Sensing
authors: Yunshu Chen, Qing Xue, Chongjun Ouyang, Zhidu Li, Yi Wang, Meng Hua
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a cornerstone of sixth-generation (6G) networks, yet conventional fixed-antenna systems lack the spatial adaptability to cope with dynamic users and targets. The emerging pinching antenna (PA) offers a flexible, low-cost solution by dynamically reconfiguring radiation points along waveguides, introducing large-scale spatial degrees of freedom. This article develops a unified architectural perspective for PA-enabled ISAC. We first discuss the unique advantages of PAs over existing flexible solutions, and then propose a PA-enabled ISAC framework that accommodates both uplink and downlink communication while being compatible with passive and active sensing targets. Within this framework, we identify representative application scenarios, discuss major design challenges, and highlight critical enabling techniques. A numerical case study demonstrates how PA reconfigurability affects the communication-sensing rate trade-off. We also outline open issues to guide further PA-ISAC research for future 6G networks.
tldr: This article presents a unified architectural framework for pinching-antenna-enabled integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) in 6G networks, covering design challenges, enabling techniques, and a numerical study of the communication-sensing rate trade-off.
motivation: Conventional fixed-antenna ISAC systems lack the spatial adaptability needed to serve dynamic users and sensing targets, so flexible, low-cost antenna solutions are sought for 6G.
method: The authors argue for pinching antennas (PAs) that dynamically reconfigure radiation points along waveguides, and propose a PA-enabled ISAC framework spanning uplink/downlink communication and passive/active sensing, supported by a numerical case study.
result: The numerical case study illustrates how PA reconfigurability shapes the trade-off between communication and sensing rates within the proposed framework.
conclusion: PA-ISAC is positioned as a promising architectural direction for 6G, with several open research issues identified to guide future work.

title: Optimal Network Dependence In Distributed Stochastic Optimization Via Tree Routing
authors: Shi Pu Runze You
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Communication is a central bottleneck in distributed optimization, but its effect is often summarized by the spectral gap of a chosen mixing matrix. Since this gap depends on link weights as well as topology, it can obscure the intrinsic effect of the network. We clarify this distinction by relating graph diameter to the inverse spectral gap. We establish a universal one-sided bound that is tight up to constant factors, while constructions across several graph families show that no topology-only converse or universal two-sided scaling law exists. This motivates a class-based view of network optimality: diameter-dependent guarantees can be assessed uniformly over graph classes, whereas spectral-gap optimality requires both the graph--matrix pair class and the admissible algorithm class to be specified. Based on the resulting diameter-based minimax benchmark, we introduce Tree-Routed Gradient Tracking (Tree-RGT), a distributed method for stochastic nonconvex optimization. The method pipelines model dissemination and gradient aggregation over a rooted shortest-path spanning tree. Each iteration uses one round of one-hop communication and one stochastic-gradient evaluation per agent, without inner consensus or multi-gossip. Under smoothness and unbiased bounded-variance oracles, Tree-RGT achieves uniformly optimal network dependence over connected graphs of prescribed size and diameter. It recovers centralized stochastic scaling after [MATH] transient iterations, where [MATH] is the number of agents and [MATH] is the graph diameter. This network-dependent transient-iteration bound improves upon or matches those reported for representative distributed methods. Thus, topology-aware routing attains diameter-optimal guarantees without relying on a prescribed mixing matrix.
tldr: The paper introduces Tree-Routed Gradient Tracking (Tree-RGT), a distributed stochastic nonconvex optimization method whose network dependence is governed by graph diameter rather than spectral gap, achieving diameter-optimal guarantees across connected graphs.
motivation: In distributed optimization, communication cost is typically captured by the spectral gap of a mixing matrix, which conflates link weights with topology and obscures the intrinsic effect of the network structure.
method: The authors relate graph diameter to the inverse spectral gap via a universal one-sided bound and show no topology-only converse exists, then propose Tree-RGT, which pipelines model dissemination and gradient aggregation over a rooted shortest-path spanning tree with one communication round and one stochastic gradient per agent per iteration.
result: Under smoothness and unbiased bounded-variance oracles, Tree-RGT achieves uniformly optimal network dependence over connected graphs of prescribed size and diameter, recovering centralized stochastic scaling after a transient of order (number of agents) × (diameter) iterations.
conclusion: Topology-aware tree routing attains diameter-optimal guarantees without relying on a prescribed mixing matrix, motivating a class-based view of network optimality for distributed optimization.

title: The Role Of Bifurcations In Parameter Estimation: A Uq Analysis Of The Non-spatial Klausmeier Model
authors: Lisa Beer, Christian Kuehn, Chiara Piazzola
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We employ uncertainty quantification methods to investigate how parameter identifiability changes in the vicinity of a bifurcation point. We perform numerical experiments on the non-spatial Klausmeier vegetation model with random coefficients, which describes biomass-water interactions and exhibits a fold bifurcation. We partition the domain around the bifurcation into regions with distinct convergence behaviors. In each region, we follow a UQ workflow that includes sensitivity analysis, Bayesian inference, and Fisher information evaluation to assess parameter identifiability. The results show that proximity to the bifurcation point is decisive for parameter estimation. Reliable joint inference of both model parameters is not possible when the system exhibits bistability. Furthermore, we can reconstruct the model's bifurcation pattern by Fisher information heatmaps, presenting a practical tool for bifurcation detection. Lastly, we highlight the importance of transient data for successful parameter estimation.
tldr: Uncertainty quantification of the non-spatial Klausmeier model shows that proximity to a fold bifurcation strongly affects parameter identifiability, with Fisher information heatmaps reconstructing the bifurcation pattern.
motivation: Parameter identifiability often degrades near bifurcations, but the precise role of bifurcation proximity in parameter estimation is not fully understood.
method: The authors perform numerical experiments on the non-spatial Klausmeier vegetation model with random coefficients, applying sensitivity analysis, Bayesian inference, and Fisher information evaluation in distinct regions around the bifurcation.
result: Reliable joint inference of both model parameters is impossible in the bistable regime, Fisher information heatmaps can reconstruct the bifurcation pattern, and transient data are crucial for successful parameter estimation.
conclusion: Proximity to the bifurcation point is decisive for parameter estimation, and Fisher information heatmaps offer a practical tool for bifurcation detection.

title: Witness Encryption Via Prime-Order Generic Groups
authors: Amit Sahai Isaac M Hair
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18275v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We unconditionally construct witness encryption for NP in the classical generic-group model, using an ordinary cyclic group of prime order. For SAT instances of size [MATH], the encryption algorithm runs in time poly[MATH], and any satisfying assignment can be used to decrypt in poly[MATH] time with correctness error [MATH]. If no satisfying assignment exists, then every generic adversary making at most [MATH] group queries has distinguishing advantage at most [MATH]. Along the way, we prove the first superconstant-factor NP-hardness of approximation result for homogeneous MinRank under randomized polynomial-time reductions, achieving a logarithmic gap even when the rank-one witness has a Boolean right factor.
tldr: The paper unconditionally constructs witness encryption for NP in the classical generic-group model using prime-order cyclic groups.
motivation: Witness encryption is a powerful cryptographic primitive, but unconditional constructions have been elusive; this work aims to achieve it in the generic-group model.
method: The authors work in the classical generic-group model with an ordinary prime-order cyclic group and provide a construction whose security relies on generic adversaries making limited group queries.
result: They obtain a witness encryption scheme for SAT instances with poly-time encryption/decryption and negligible distinguishing advantage for generic adversaries, and also prove NP-hardness of approximation for homogeneous MinRank with a logarithmic gap.
conclusion: The work advances classical cryptography and complexity theory but has no direct connection to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: The Verifiable Action Card: Trustworthy Human-in-the-Loop Control For Secure Autonomous Agents
authors: Hasnain Irshad, Anam Mughees, Neelam Mughees, Abdullah Mughees, Imtiaz Ali Soomro
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic browsers can execute security-sensitive actions under a user's authenticated session, making indirect prompt injection and deceptive confirmation interfaces a direct threat to action integrity. Existing human-in-the-loop (HITL) safeguards are insufficient when the approval prompt itself can be influenced by untrusted page content or model-generated text. We present the (VAC), an architectural defence that reconstructs approval information from the ground-truth pending browser action and trusted intent provenance, renders it out-of-band in the trusted browser chrome, and binds approval to the exact action re-verified at dispatch. VAC combines provenance fencing, a ground-truth action descriptor, default-deny confirmation, provenance-aware risk gating, and execution binding. We implement VAC in a complete agentic browser and evaluate it on a 24-scenario benchmark covering confused-deputy attacks, Lies-in-the-Loop dialog forging, indirect prompt injection, adaptive action substitution, provenance evasion, and legitimate tasks. Across the evaluated LLMs, attack success without VAC ranges from [MATH] to [MATH], whereas VAC reduces attack success to [MATH] on every model, with [MATH] legitimate-task completion and a [MATH] false-block rate. These results show that grounding approval in the action that will actually execute provides architectural protection against security failures that prompt-level defences and conventional HITL confirmation cannot reliably prevent.
tldr: The paper proposes the Verifiable Action Card (VAC), an architectural defence for agentic browsers that grounds human-in-the-loop approval in the ground-truth pending action and binds execution to a re-verified action descriptor.
motivation: Agentic browsers can execute security-sensitive actions under authenticated sessions, but existing HITL safeguards fail when approval prompts are influenced by untrusted page content or model-generated text, enabling indirect prompt injection and deceptive confirmation attacks.
method: VAC combines provenance fencing, a ground-truth action descriptor, default-deny confirmation, provenance-aware risk gating, and execution binding, rendered out-of-band in trusted browser chrome.
result: Evaluated on a 24-scenario benchmark across several LLMs, VAC reduces attack success to 0% on every model while maintaining high legitimate-task completion and a low false-block rate.
conclusion: Grounding approval in the action that will actually execute provides architectural protection against security failures that prompt-level defences and conventional HITL confirmation cannot reliably prevent.

title: On Fluctuations Of The Drift In Hyperbolic Groups
authors: Manuel Stadlbauer Gil Jos\'e Astudillo Hernandez
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] refer to a convex-cocompact group of isometries of a CAT([MATH]) space [MATH] and [MATH] to a Galois cover with a word-hyperbolic group of deck transformations. We show that, for almost every geodesic [MATH] with respect to the Bowen-Margulis-Sullivan measure on the lift of [MATH], there exist [MATH] and a standard Brownian motion [MATH] such that, for any [MATH], \[ d(p(g_s (\xi)), ) = s + \sigma B_s + o(s^\lambda), \] with [MATH] referring to the geodesic flow acting on the geodesics of [MATH] and [MATH] to the canonical projection to [MATH]. The result is a consequence of an almost sure invariance principle for random walks on hyperbolic groups with dependent increments, whose proof makes use of a new Ruelle operator theorem for skew products and Martin boundary techniques for random walks with dependent increments.
tldr: The paper establishes an almost sure invariance principle for random walks on hyperbolic groups with dependent increments, yielding a Brownian-motion description of drift fluctuations along geodesics for convex-cocompact groups acting on CAT(0) spaces.
motivation: The authors aim to understand the asymptotic fluctuations of the geodesic drift in negatively curved / hyperbolic geometric settings, extending classical fluctuation results to random walks with dependent increments.
method: They prove a new Ruelle operator theorem for skew products and use Martin boundary techniques for random walks with dependent increments to derive the almost sure invariance principle.
result: For almost every geodesic with respect to the Bowen-Margulis-Sullivan measure, the projected distance grows as s + sigma B_s + o(s^lambda), where B_s is a standard Brownian motion.
conclusion: The work provides a strong probabilistic limit theorem (a.s. invariance principle) for hyperbolic groups and CAT(0) spaces, with tools (skew-product Ruelle operators, Martin boundaries) likely useful for further ergodic-theoretic studies.

title: Electrostatic Quadrupole Lens For Focusing A Cryogenic $^{205}$TlF Molecular Beam
authors: Pengyu Zhou, Olivier Grasdijk, David Demille, Jakob Kastelic, David Kawall, Jianhui Li, Oskari Timgren, Konrad Wenz, Yuanhang Yang, Tanya Zelevinsky
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17915v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Precision measurements with molecules require molecular beams with high flux and narrow divergence. Here we present the design, implementation, and characterization of an electrostatic quadrupole lens (EQL) for focusing a cryogenic beam of [MATH]TlF molecules. The EQL consists of four electrodes operated at spatially alternating potentials up to [MATH] kV. This configuration generates a transverse restoring force that focuses molecules prepared in selected manifold of hyperfine states. At the optimal applied voltage, the EQL increases the detected molecular signal by a factor of [MATH] at the current detection position. The measured lens gain, transverse Doppler spectra, and transverse spatial profiles are all reproduced by trajectory simulations using independently measured beam parameters as input. Based on this agreement, we project a gain of [MATH] for the full [MATH] CeNTREX beamline. These results establish the EQL as a key component for increasing sensitivity in precision experiments using cryogenic beams of polar molecules.
tldr: Design and characterization of an electrostatic quadrupole lens for focusing a cryogenic 205TlF molecular beam to enhance precision measurements.
motivation: Precision experiments with polar molecules require high-flux, low-divergence molecular beams, and focusing can increase detected signal and sensitivity.
method: A four-electrode electrostatic quadrupole lens with spatially alternating potentials focuses molecules in selected hyperfine states; trajectory simulations using measured beam parameters are compared with measured lens gain, transverse Doppler spectra, and spatial profiles.
result: At optimal voltage, the lens increases the detected molecular signal by a factor, and simulations reproduce the measurements, projecting a further gain for the full CeNTREX beamline.
conclusion: The electrostatic quadrupole lens is established as a key component for increasing sensitivity in precision experiments using cryogenic beams of polar molecules.

title: Wavelength-Multiplexed Nonlinear Computing With A Single-Layer Diffractive Optical Processor
authors: Yongkang Cheng, Che-Yung Shen, Yuntian Wang, Shiqi Chen, Aydogan Ozcan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffractive optical processors provide a promising platform for high-throughput, low-latency analog computing by exploiting engineered wave propagation to transform optical fields. However, implementing nonlinear mappings in optical hardware remains challenging. Here, we introduce a wavelength-multiplexed encoding-and-decoding (E+D) diffractive processor that exploits multiple illumination wavelengths to enhance the nonlinear function-approximation capability of a compact single-layer diffractive architecture, without cascading multiple diffractive layers or increasing the trainable degrees of freedom. Under sequential wavelength scanning, each wavelength-detector channel implements a distinct nonlinear function at the output of the diffractive processor. Numerical simulations using 100 wavelength channels and 10,000 spatial detector regions at the output of the diffractive processor demonstrate the implementation of one million distinct nonlinear functions through wavelength multiplexing. We also demonstrate a simultaneous multiwavelength illumination configuration in which the E+D diffractive processor performs wavelength-division multiplexing and nonlinear function approximation concurrently. This multiwavelength illumination configuration is experimentally validated by optically implementing 64 distinct nonlinear functions under simultaneous illumination at eight wavelengths from 495 to 635 nm. Through numerical simulations and visible-light experimental demonstrations, our results indicate that this wavelength-multiplexed nonlinear function approximation framework provides a scalable route toward compact, high-capacity diffractive processors for large-scale analog optical computing and optical information processing.
tldr: A single-layer diffractive optical processor using wavelength multiplexing performs many distinct nonlinear function approximations without cascading layers or increasing trainable degrees of freedom.
motivation: Implementing nonlinear mappings in optical hardware is challenging, and existing diffractive processors typically require multiple cascaded layers to achieve nonlinear function approximation.
method: The authors introduce a wavelength-multiplexed encoding-and-decoding diffractive processor that exploits multiple illumination wavelengths to enhance nonlinear approximation capability, and they validate it numerically and experimentally.
result: Numerical simulations with 100 wavelength channels and 10,000 detector regions demonstrate one million distinct nonlinear functions, and experiments with eight visible wavelengths implement 64 distinct nonlinear functions under simultaneous illumination.
conclusion: Wavelength multiplexing offers a scalable route to compact, high-capacity diffractive processors for large-scale analog optical computing and optical information processing.

title: Fenchel-Young Duality Gaps: Certified Early Stopping For Regularized Inverse Problems
authors: Pierre-Cyril Aubin-Frankowski (CERMICS UMR 9032, ENPC), Yohann de Castro
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study computable error bounds and certified early stopping for regularized inverse problems, where a data-fidelity term is traded against a regularizer. The analysis relies on an exact duality-gap identity that splits the total gap of [MATH] into a data-fidelity Fenchel--Young loss and a regularizer Fenchel--Young loss, [MATH] valid for any primal point [MATH] and any dual point [MATH]. The data-fidelity term [MATH] is strictly convex, so wherever [MATH] is differentiable the loss [MATH] is the Bregman divergence of~[MATH] between the prediction [MATH] and [MATH], and it vanishes exactly at [MATH]. Evaluated at a dual-feasible point [MATH], the gap~[MATH] is computable and , meaning that it uses no knowledge of the solution, and it bounds the suboptimality of [MATH]. Under the source condition, the same Fenchel--Young losses give bounds on the estimation and prediction errors. Their scale is the irreducible model and noise error [MATH], which vanishes exactly when Mirror Alignment holds at the certificate. This gives an early-stopping rule: run the algorithm until the regularizer Fenchel--Young loss falls below a tolerance [MATH]. A constructive version of the Br\o ndsted--Rockafellar theorem then turns the current pair into an exact one, and this proxy lifts to an exact primal certificate. We build the proxy by a proximal step in the geometry of the fidelity, with Bregman kernel [MATH] and tilted by the prediction [MATH]: it recovers the Euclidean step of Carlier when [MATH] is the squared error, and it reduces the duality gap by the regularizer Fenchel--Young loss, up to a second-order remainder that vanishes in the quadratic case. Our running example is the Generalized Beurling--Lasso (GBL), where [MATH] is the total-variation norm on signed measures. It contains the classical Beurling--Lasso, obtained with the squared error, and also covers robust, logistic, entropic and inverse-optimal-transport losses. The same duality gap certifies deep-learning optimizers such as Lion-K and Muon, in their proximal form, as solvers of the regularized program. A companion paper by the same authors builds on these error bounds to establish exact support recovery for the GBL under a non-degenerate source condition.
tldr: The paper derives exact Fenchel-Young duality-gap identities to provide computable error bounds and certified early stopping for regularized inverse problems.
motivation: Regularized inverse problems require practical certificates for when an iterative solver has converged or when to stop, without access to the unknown solution.
method: It splits the duality gap into data-fidelity and regularizer Fenchel-Young losses, uses Bregman divergences and a proximal step in the fidelity geometry to construct a computable proxy certificate.
result: The computable gap bounds suboptimality and supports an early-stopping rule; a constructive Brøndsted-Rockafellar theorem lifts the proxy to an exact primal certificate, illustrated by Generalized Beurling-Lasso and deep-learning optimizers.
conclusion: The framework yields certified early stopping and error bounds for a broad class of regularized inverse problems, including robust, logistic, entropic, and inverse-optimal-transport losses.

title: On The Computational Cost Of Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics
authors: Mateusz B. Majka, Tigran Nagapetyan, {\l}ukasz Szpruch, Yue Wu, Danqi Zhuang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17750v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) reduces the cost of Langevin-based sampling by replacing full-dataset drift evaluations with mini-batch approximations, but the resulting subsampling error may offset this computational saving. We study this trade-off for stochastic differential equations with finite-sum drifts and compare the computational cost of SGLD with that of the Euler-Maruyama (EM) method. For a prescribed mean-square accuracy [MATH], we derive complexity estimates that explicitly track the dependence on the dataset size [MATH], mini-batch size [MATH], and accuracy parameter [MATH]. The resulting comparison reveals distinct parameter regimes in which either method is preferable. In particular, EM can have lower leading-order cost only in a small-data, aggressive-subsampling regime, whereas SGLD is favoured over most of the remaining parameter space. In the practically relevant regime [MATH], the transition between the two methods occurs at the scale [MATH]. We complement the theoretical analysis with numerical experiments based on a Gaussian Bayesian inference model, which examine the predicted cost regimes together with the underlying discretisation error and variance estimates.
tldr: The paper analyzes the computational cost trade-off between Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) and Euler-Maruyama (EM) for stochastic differential equations with finite-sum drifts.
motivation: SGLD reduces per-iteration cost via mini-batch drift approximations, but subsampling error may negate savings, motivating a rigorous complexity comparison against full-batch EM sampling.
method: The authors derive mean-square complexity estimates that explicitly track dataset size, mini-batch size, and accuracy, then validate the predicted cost regimes with numerical experiments on a Gaussian Bayesian inference model.
result: Distinct parameter regimes favor either method: EM has lower leading-order cost only in a small-data, aggressive-subsampling regime, whereas SGLD is preferred over most of the parameter space, with a transition at a specified scale in the practically relevant regime.
conclusion: The work provides a precise cost comparison that guides method selection for Langevin-based sampling with finite-sum drifts.

title: Spatio-temporal Latent Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models For Reduced-order Modeling Of Parametrized Dynamical Systems
authors: Michiel Nikken, Nicol\`o Botteghi, Federico Califano, Silke Glas
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many scientific problems require accurate modeling of complex physical phenomena, such as fluid dynamics or climate modeling. These phenomena often result in high-dimensional and thus computationally expensive computational models that can limit their application to real-time and multi-query problems. Model-order reduction (MOR) is an approach that seeks to approximate full-order models (FOMs) using reduced-order models (ROMs), trading a minor reduction in accuracy for a major reduction in computational cost. In this work, we propose a non-intrusive MOR method using generative machine learning by means of denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) for generating solutions of the dynamical systems under different instances of their parameters. Unlike conventional DDPMs, which often operate purely in the spatial domain, we aim to generate spatio-temporal solutions to improve quality and temporal coherence. In addition, we embed the DDPM in a latent space obtained by sequentially applying proper orthogonal decomposition and an autoencoder to reduce the data dimensionality and the computational cost of the DDPM. We test our approach on a parametrized 2D fluid flow around an obstacle. The numerical experiments demonstrate that our latent DDPM can (i) produce accurate and temporally coherent solutions, (ii) achieve strong generalization capabilities to scenarios involving unseen parameter values, and (iii) extrapolate in time beyond the training horizon.
tldr: The paper proposes a non-intrusive reduced-order modeling framework that uses latent spatio-temporal denoising diffusion probabilistic models to generate solutions of parametrized dynamical systems, demonstrated on 2D fluid flow around an obstacle.
motivation: High-fidelity simulations of complex physical phenomena such as fluid dynamics and climate modeling are high-dimensional and computationally expensive, which limits their use in real-time and multi-query settings. Model-order reduction offers a way to trade slight accuracy loss for large computational savings.
method: The authors combine proper orthogonal decomposition and an autoencoder to build a low-dimensional latent space, then train a denoising diffusion probabilistic model that generates spatio-temporal solutions conditioned on system parameters, improving temporal coherence over purely spatial DDPMs.
result: On a parametrized 2D flow-around-obstacle benchmark, the latent DDPM produces accurate and temporally coherent solutions, generalizes to unseen parameter values, and extrapolates in time beyond the training horizon.
conclusion: Latent spatio-temporal diffusion models provide an effective non-intrusive surrogate for parametrized dynamical systems, though the work is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: The Erd\H{o}s--S\'os Theorem
authors: David R. Wood
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an exposition of a proof, discovered by GPT-6 Astra, of the Erds--S\'os Conjecture, which states that every graph with average degree greater than [MATH] contains every tree on [MATH] vertices.
tldr: This paper presents an exposition of a proof of the Erdős–Sós conjecture in graph theory, stating that every graph with average degree greater than k−1 contains every tree on k vertices.
motivation: The Erdős–Sós conjecture is a longstanding open problem in extremal graph theory, and the paper aims to make a newly discovered proof accessible through exposition.
method: The work provides an expository proof, attributed to GPT-6 Astra, of the Erdős–Sós conjecture for trees in graphs with sufficiently large average degree.
result: It verifies the conjecture that average degree greater than k−1 forces the existence of every k-vertex tree as a subgraph.
conclusion: The paper is a purely graph-theoretic contribution with no connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: The Bar-sot Method: Long-term Average Cost Control As Stochastic Optimal Self-Transport
authors: Sharan Srinivasan, Berke M. Turkay, Harsha Honnappa
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We reformulate average-cost (ergodic) control of a Markov jump process as a finite-horizon stochastic optimal transport (SOT) problem that jointly optimizes over the controlled evolution and the marginal law from which it starts and returns to (i.e., a self-transport). The constraint relating the marginal flow to the controlled generator is the basic adjoint relationship (BAR), so we call the resulting problem BAR-SOT. For any time horizon T>0, its optimal value is a constant scaling of the long-run average-cost rate. We give three equivalent formulations (through controlled processes, a Fokker--Planck constraint, and relaxed marginal measures) and show that the optimal dual is a stationary potential plus a term linear in time, with slope equal to the rate. A relative-entropy penalty on the control yields a cost-tilted Schrodinger bridge problem, computable by a Sinkhorn-type iteration when every transition rate is controlled, whose value converges to the unregularized optimum as the penalty vanishes. We develop the theory for finite Markov decision processes and then for general controlled Markov jump processes. A neural parametrization of the dual, trained as a physics-informed neural network (PINN), that encodes Harrison's equivalent-workload formulation (see Harrison 2000) matches the strong reinforcement-learning baseline of Dai and Gluzman (2022); numerically conditioning the fit of a sub-dominant transverse correction then improves on both that baseline and the best priority heuristic. On the input-queued switch, a graph-attention parametrization of the dual improves on the strongest matching heuristic we are aware of, with a parameter count that does not grow with the switch size.
tldr: The paper reformulates average-cost control of Markov jump processes as a stochastic optimal transport problem with a self-transport constraint, providing dual formulations and neural/PINN-based solutions.
motivation: Long-run average-cost control of Markov jump processes is central to queueing and network control, but existing methods lack a unified optimal-transport perspective that can leverage modern computational tools.
method: The authors introduce the BAR-SOT formulation, show equivalence to controlled processes, Fokker-Planck constraints, and relaxed marginal measures, derive a dual with a stationary potential plus linear time term, and add a relative-entropy penalty yielding a cost-tilted Schrödinger bridge solvable by Sinkhorn-type iterations.
result: They develop the theory for finite MDPs and general controlled Markov jump processes, and demonstrate that a PINN-parametrized dual matches or improves strong reinforcement-learning and heuristic baselines on input-queued switches with parameter count independent of switch size.
conclusion: The BAR-SOT framework offers a principled and scalable approach to average-cost control, connecting stochastic optimal transport, Schrödinger bridges, and neural dual parametrization with competitive empirical performance.

title: A Factorization Method For Support Recovery In Magnetic Induction Tomography
authors: Chengzhe Jiang Junqing Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a factorization framework for magnetic induction tomography in the eddy-current regime. The induced current density is represented by a divergence-free current vector potential, and the external excitation by magnetic dipole densities on an observation sphere. This choice reveals a natural physical factorization of the near-field operator into a data operator, an interior boundary response operator, and an adjoint counterpart. By introducing the Riesz map on the flux space, we recast this factorization in a Hilbert-space setting, which yields a positive-semidefinite operator with a coercive middle factor. Douglas' range theorem then identifies the range of the square root of this dissipative operator with the range of the data operator. For inclusions with a regular boundary, this range identity yields a uniqueness theorem for the support of the conductivity. This characterization leads to a non-iterative spectral indicator based on a regularized Picard quotient computed from the Hermitian imaginary part of the near-field data matrix. The reconstruction stage requires no forward solves. Numerical experiments confirm that the indicator localizes and separates the inclusions accurately, degrades gracefully under increasing noise, and captures non-convex support geometry without any convexity prior.
tldr: The paper develops a factorization framework for magnetic induction tomography in the eddy-current regime, yielding a non-iterative spectral indicator for recovering the support of conductivity inclusions.
motivation: Magnetic induction tomography is a non-invasive imaging modality whose inverse problem is nonlinear and ill-posed, so efficient and provably convergent support-recovery methods are of practical interest.
method: The induced current is represented via a divergence-free vector potential and the excitation via magnetic dipole densities, factorizing the near-field operator into data, interior boundary response, and adjoint operators; a Riesz map recasts this in Hilbert space, and Douglas' range theorem identifies the range of the square root of the resulting dissipative operator.
result: For inclusions with regular boundary the range identity yields a uniqueness theorem for the conductivity support, and the resulting regularized Picard-quotient spectral indicator localizes and separates inclusions without forward solves, degrading gracefully under noise and capturing non-convex geometry.
conclusion: The factorization approach provides a rigorous theoretical basis and an effective non-iterative reconstruction scheme for magnetic induction tomography, with numerical experiments supporting the analysis.

title: Surjective Hausdorff Isometries Of Hyperspaces Of Bounded Closed Convex Sets
authors: Lixin Cheng, Wuyi He, Chulei Liu, Zheming Zheng
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] and [MATH] be real Banach spaces, and let [MATH] and [MATH] denote the families of all nonempty bounded closed convex subsets of [MATH] and [MATH], respectively, equipped with the Hausdorff metric. We prove that every surjective isometry [MATH] is induced by a surjective affine isometry of the underlying spaces. More precisely, [MATH] maps singleton sets onto singleton sets, and the map [MATH] defined by [MATH] is a surjective affine isometry satisfying \[ F(A)=T[A]:=\{T(x):\;x\in A\},\qquad(A\in\cC(X)). \] In particular, our theorem extends the result of Gruber and Lettl for finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces to arbitrary real Banach spaces, without imposing any additional assumptions on the underlying spaces.
tldr: The paper characterizes surjective isometries between hyperspaces of nonempty bounded closed convex subsets of real Banach spaces under the Hausdorff metric, proving they are induced by surjective affine isometries of the underlying spaces.
motivation: The result extends the Gruber-Lettl theorem from finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces to arbitrary real Banach spaces without additional assumptions.
method: The authors use methods from nonlinear functional analysis and metric geometry, analyzing the action of a surjective isometry on the family of bounded closed convex sets and showing it preserves singleton sets.
result: Every such surjective isometry maps singleton sets to singleton sets and is induced by a surjective affine isometry T, so that F(A) = T[A] for all A.
conclusion: This generalizes prior finite-dimensional results to all real Banach spaces, providing a structural theorem for isometries of convex hyperspaces.

title: Trust Propagation And Structural Containment In Multi-agent Llm Pipelines
authors: Tanzim Hossain Safin, Sharif Noor Zisad, Swakkhar Shatabda, Ragib Hasan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly automate tasks involving agents with different levels of privilege, creating a security risk in which a compromised low-privilege agent can influence a higher-privilege agent and trigger an unauthorized action. We study attack propagation in a four-agent LangGraph pipeline comprising a Supervisor, Researcher, Validator, and Executor. We evaluate shared-memory poisoning and indirect prompt injection through a forged approval embedded in a retrieved document. We compare the Validator's judgment with an independent authorization layer using task-bound signed tokens and a separately verified policy oracle. Our contribution is an empirical study of attack propagation, a component-level ablation of the authorization boundary, and the Judgment Bypass Rate (JBR), which measures compromise at the attacked agent rather than at the final action. Across three seeds and 60 labeled tasks, memory poisoning reaches execution in every undefended trial. With authorization enabled, it achieves 100% JBR but 0% Unsafe Action Rate, showing that the Validator can remain compromised while execution is contained. Against an attacker possessing the signing secret, the policy oracle provides the observed containment, while an independently authored least privilege policy preserves this result. An Observer layer reduces the false-positive rate for agent hijacking from 49% to 7% without weakening execution-level security. These results show that structural authorization can contain compromised agent behavior even when upstream LLM judgment fails.
