abstract: ArXiv:2609.18183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The properties of water under high pressure and high temperature (HP-HT) are critical in multiple geochemical processes in deep Earth. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) is a promising approach to study water under extreme conditions without any empirical parameters. However, the accuracy of AIMD simulations is determined by the exchange-correlation (XC) functional including the dispersion correction used in density functional theory calculations. While van der Waals (vdW) interactions are well known to be critically important for water under ambient conditions, the influence of the dispersion correction on the properties of HP-HT water as found in Earth's mantle remains largely unexplored. To address this, we carried out AIMD simulations for supercritical water at 1, 5, and 10 GPa, and 1000 K. We compared PBE, PBE-D3, RPBE-D3, and SCAN functionals, where D3 means Grimme's D3 dispersion correction. We compared the structural, diffusion, and vibrational properties of water as computed with these XC functionals. Overall, the discrepancies between the functionals are reduced under extreme P-T conditions relative to ambient conditions. PBE and PBE-D3 exhibit higher proton-transfer rates than RPBE-D3 and SCAN, suggesting that while vdW interactions do not significantly affect the water structure under extreme conditions, the oxygen-hydrogen bond strength does influence proton transfer. Our results provide molecular-level insight into water in Earth's mantle and offer valuable guidance for selecting appropriate XC functionals in AIMD simulations of aqueous solutions under extreme conditions.
tldr: AIMD simulations compare exchange-correlation functionals to study how van der Waals interactions affect the structure, diffusion, and proton transfer of supercritical water under Earth's mantle conditions.
motivation: The accuracy of ab initio molecular dynamics for water at high pressure and temperature depends on the exchange-correlation functional and dispersion correction, but the influence of van der Waals interactions on HP-HT water relevant to Earth's mantle is largely unexplored.
method: The authors performed AIMD simulations of supercritical water at 1, 5, and 10 GPa and 1000 K, comparing PBE, PBE-D3, RPBE-D3, and SCAN functionals, and analyzed structural, diffusion, and vibrational properties.
result: Discrepancies between functionals are reduced under extreme P-T conditions compared to ambient conditions; PBE and PBE-D3 show higher proton-transfer rates than RPBE-D3 and SCAN, indicating that vdW interactions do not significantly affect water structure but O-H bond strength influences proton transfer.
conclusion: The results provide molecular-level insight into water in Earth's mantle and guidance for selecting XC functionals in AIMD simulations of aqueous solutions under extreme conditions.

title: Prior-Aided Masked Vector Quantization Csi Feedback For Fdd Massive Mimo Systems
authors: Yi Song, Tianyu Yang, Kangda Zhi, Shuangyang Li, Fangzhou Wu, Songyan Xue, Giuseppe Caire
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Downlink channel state information (CSI) feedback is a key bottleneck in frequency-division duplex (FDD) massive MIMO systems, as the user equipment (UE) must convey its estimated channel to the base station (BS) over a limited uplink (UL) budget. To improve CSI reconstruction accuracy under tight feedback constraints, we propose prior-aided masked vector quantization (PM-VQ), a learning-based separate source--channel coding (SSCC) feedback scheme conditioned on the average angle--delay power map---a compact representation of the channel second-order statistics available at both the UE and the BS. In PM-VQ, a prior-aided encoder maps the CSI to latent tokens, and a spatially-adaptive masking module (SAMM) scores and selects the most informative tokens within the feedback budget. The selected tokens are vector-quantized and fed back together with their positions, while an adaptive de-masking module (ADM) completes the latent representation at the BS before prior-conditioned decoding. To support variable-rate compression, a single model is trained over a range of selected-token counts, enabling operation across multiple feedback dimensions without retraining. We evaluate PM-VQ against three representative baselines on a Sionna-generated 3GPP TR~38.901 UMa dataset, focusing on the most challenging diffuse regime where channel energy is spread across many angle--delay coefficients. Simulation results show that PM-VQ achieves the lowest NMSE across all tested SNR levels and feedback dimensions in this regime. Moreover, the angle--delay power-map prior remains beneficial even when estimated from only a few channel realizations.
tldr: The paper proposes prior-aided masked vector quantization (PM-VQ) for CSI feedback in FDD massive MIMO systems, using a learned separate source-channel coding scheme to improve reconstruction under tight feedback budgets.
motivation: Downlink CSI feedback is a bottleneck in FDD massive MIMO, and accurate reconstruction under limited uplink resources remains challenging, especially in diffuse regimes where channel energy is spread across many angle-delay coefficients.
method: PM-VQ uses a prior-aided encoder, a spatially-adaptive masking module to select informative latent tokens within a feedback budget, vector quantization of selected tokens, and an adaptive de-masking module with prior-conditioned decoding; a single model supports variable rates.
result: On a Sionna-generated 3GPP TR 38.901 UMa dataset, PM-VQ achieves the lowest NMSE across all tested SNR levels and feedback dimensions in the diffuse regime, and the angle-delay power-map prior remains beneficial even when estimated from few channel realizations.
conclusion: The proposed learning-based SSCC feedback scheme effectively improves CSI reconstruction accuracy in challenging FDD massive MIMO scenarios, with practical benefits from a compact statistical prior.

title: A Universal Characterisation Of The Bochner Integral
authors: Jean-David Jacques, Felix Medwed, Fabrizio Zanello
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide a universal characterisation of the Banach spaces of equivalence classes of [MATH] Bochner integrable functions, under equality almost everywhere, as initial objects in appropriate categories of bifunctors, for all [MATH]. As a by-product of our construction, we also obtain a unique characterisation of the Bochner integral.
tldr: The paper gives a universal categorical characterization of Bochner-integrable function spaces and the Bochner integral itself.
motivation: The authors aim to understand the Bochner integral through a universal property, extending categorical characterizations from simpler integration theories.
method: They construct categories of bifunctors and show that Banach spaces of equivalence classes of Bochner integrable functions are initial objects, yielding a unique characterization of the integral.
result: A universal characterization of these Banach spaces as initial objects in appropriate categories is obtained, along with a unique characterization of the Bochner integral.
conclusion: This work provides a category-theoretic foundation for the Bochner integral, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Matching Multi-Loop Complexities With A Single Loop: Optimal Optimization Stationarity And Best-Known Game Stationarity In Nonconvex--Concave Minimax Optimization
authors: Zi Xu Minghao Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a new single-loop algorithmic framework for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax optimization. The resulting projected damped extragradient method combines projected extragradient updates, dual momentum, and a moving proximal center. Under both the optimization-stationarity and game-stationarity criteria, our method achieves the best-known complexity among single-loop first-order methods. For optimization stationarity, our method achieves a gradient complexity of [MATH], where [MATH] is the gradient Lipschitz constant, [MATH] bounds the diameter of the dual feasible set, and [MATH] is an initialization quantity involving the value-function gap and the initial gradients. Moreover, by incorporating a fixed-center warm-up phase, the complexity can be improved to [MATH], up to an additive lower-order cost, where [MATH]. We further establish a lower bound of [MATH] for optimization stationarity over projected zero-respecting first-order methods. This lower bound proves that the warm-started version of our algorithm is optimal up to a constant factor for optimization stationarity within this oracle class. For game stationarity, our method achieves [MATH] gradient complexity. This matches the best-known complexity of multi-loop first-order methods, thereby establishing the same complexity with a single-loop algorithmic structure. Under dual strong concavity, the proposed framework achieves [MATH] leading complexity for both stationarity criteria, where [MATH] is the dual condition number, up to an additive initialization cost. The [MATH] accuracy dependence is optimal under fixed regularity and initialization bounds.
tldr: The paper introduces a single-loop projected damped extragradient method for smooth nonconvex–concave minimax optimization, achieving best-known complexities under optimization and game stationarity criteria.
motivation: Minimax optimization is important in machine learning and game theory, but existing optimal methods often require multi-loop structures; the authors aim to match those complexities with a simpler single-loop algorithm.
method: They propose a projected damped extragradient method combining projected extragradient updates, dual momentum, and a moving proximal center, along with a fixed-center warm-up phase and lower-bound analysis.
result: The method achieves best-known single-loop complexity for optimization stationarity, matches multi-loop complexity for game stationarity, and attains optimal accuracy dependence under dual strong concavity.
conclusion: A single-loop algorithm can match multi-loop complexities in nonconvex–concave minimax optimization, and the warm-started variant is optimal within projected zero-respecting first-order methods for optimization stationarity.

title: A Lattice Boltzmann Method With Adaptive Relaxation Parameter And Lax--Friedrichs-Type Equilibrium For Hyperbolic Systems
authors: Yifan Zhang, Ping Lin, Jin Zhao, Weifeng Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, a lattice Boltzmann method with an adaptive relaxation parameter and a Lax--Friedrichs-type equilibrium is proposed for hyperbolic systems with source terms. The equilibrium distribution recovers the conservative variables and physical fluxes while incorporating dissipation determined by characteristic-speed bounds. To balance accuracy and robustness, the relaxation parameter is selected from a local smoothness indicator based on characteristic projections. In smooth regions, the parameter approaches the low-dissipation limit, retaining second-order accuracy; near discontinuities, it is automatically reduced to introduce localized dissipation and suppress nonphysical oscillations. The stabilization acts directly through the local collision step and preserves the standard collide-and-stream structure, without a posteriori recomputation or interface-based limiting. Maxwell iteration establishes second-order consistency in smooth regions, and a weighted [MATH]-stability estimate is proved for linear hyperbolic systems with periodic boundary conditions under a standard CFL condition. Numerical experiments for scalar advection, Euler, shallow-water, and reactive Euler equations demonstrate the expected accuracy for smooth solutions and robust resolution of challenging one- and two-dimensional discontinuous problems, including wet--dry fronts and reactive discontinuities. A large-scale simulation of a 2D cellular detonation further demonstrates the capability of the method to resolve long-time multidimensional shock--reaction interactions.
tldr: The paper develops an adaptive lattice Boltzmann method with a Lax--Friedrichs-type equilibrium for solving hyperbolic systems with source terms.
motivation: The authors aim to improve the accuracy and robustness of lattice Boltzmann methods for hyperbolic conservation laws, especially near discontinuities, while preserving the standard collide-and-stream structure.
method: They propose a local smoothness indicator based on characteristic projections to adaptively select the relaxation parameter and design a Lax--Friedrichs-type equilibrium that recovers conservative variables and physical fluxes with controlled dissipation.
result: Maxwell iteration proves second-order consistency in smooth regions and an L2-stability estimate is derived for linear hyperbolic systems; numerical tests on scalar advection, Euler, shallow-water, and reactive Euler equations demonstrate accuracy and robustness.
conclusion: The method effectively balances low dissipation in smooth regions with localized stabilization near discontinuities, enabling challenging multidimensional shock-reaction simulations such as cellular detonation.

title: Weak Averaging Principle And Weak Pullback Attractors For Mckean--Vlasov Stochastic Navier--Stokes Equations
authors: Honglei Chen (school Of Mathematical Sciences, Dalian University Of Technology), Zhenxin Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish three weak averaging principles for distribution-dependent stochastic Navier--Stokes equations with rapidly oscillating coefficients on the torus [MATH]. First, solution laws are relatively compact on finite time intervals, and every limit point as [MATH] is the path law of a variational martingale solution of the averaged equation. Under a dissipative condition, we can choose bounded complete variational solution laws of the original and averaged equations so that every sequence with [MATH] has a subsequence converging weakly to a bounded complete variational solution law of the averaged equation. At the level of probability laws, the original nonautonomous equation admits a family of weak pullback attractors, while the averaged equation has a weak global attractor. The weak pullback attractors converge upper semicontinuously to the weak global attractor of the averaged equation, uniformly with respect to the coefficient hull.
tldr: The paper establishes weak averaging principles and weak pullback attractors for McKean-Vlasov stochastic Navier-Stokes equations with rapidly oscillating coefficients.
motivation: It aims to understand the averaging and long-time asymptotic behavior of distribution-dependent stochastic Navier-Stokes equations on a torus.
method: The authors use variational martingale solutions, relative compactness of solution laws, dissipative conditions, and weak pullback/global attractor theory.
result: They prove three weak averaging principles and show that the weak pullback attractors of the original equation converge upper semicontinuously to the weak global attractor of the averaged equation.
conclusion: The work provides a mathematical framework for averaging and attractor convergence in McKean-Vlasov stochastic fluid models.

title: An Efficient And Rigorous Criterion For The Admissible Time Step Of Deforming Grids In Generalized Lagrangian And Ale Methods
authors: Yicun Zhen, Shouxian Zhu, Shipeng Mao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is mathematically proved that a sufficient condition for deformed grid to remain valid is that the Jacobian determinant of the deformation remains positive within each element and the boundary is preserved under the deformation throughout the time interval. This result provides a rigorous and element-wise check method for users of the generalized Lagrangian scheme and the arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian scheme to assess grid validity.
tldr: The paper proves a sufficient condition for deforming grids to remain valid in generalized Lagrangian and arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) numerical schemes, based on positivity of the deformation Jacobian determinant within each element.
motivation: Deforming-grid numerical schemes require that the mesh remain non-degenerate (valid) throughout a simulation, but a rigorous, element-wise criterion for checking this was lacking.
method: A mathematical proof establishing that positivity of the Jacobian determinant of the deformation inside each element, combined with boundary preservation over the time interval, guarantees grid validity.
result: The authors obtain a rigorous, element-wise check that users of generalized Lagrangian and ALE schemes can apply to assess whether their grids remain valid during deformation.
conclusion: The criterion offers a practical and mathematically rigorous tool for mesh-validity assessment in Lagrangian and ALE numerical methods.

title: State Without A Landlord: An Architecture Proposal For Peer-to-Peer Replication Of Durable Workflow State
authors: Matteo Collina Luca Maraschi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Durable-execution frameworks commonly journal execution steps of a long-running function and reconstruct state by deterministic replay; the journal is therefore the workflow's authoritative state, and in current deployments it typically resides with whichever provider hosts the run. This paper examines what changes if the journal is instead an authenticated, append-only log replicated among the parties to the workflow. We propose an architecture in which runs are chains of single-writer epoch cores; executor succession is governed by quorum-finalized closure certificates; durability, timeout, and checkpoint decisions are carried by explicit certificates rather than implicit trust; and large payloads travel a separate content-addressed distribution plane. A threat model separates what signatures establish (authorship and order) from what they do not (truth of recorded effects). We state the design as a set of typed artifacts and invariants, identify which claims are established by existing systems and which are proposals requiring validation, and define the prototype experiments, including specific adversarial cases, that would validate or falsify the proposal's central mechanisms.
tldr: The paper proposes a peer-to-peer architecture for replicating durable workflow state as an authenticated append-only log among workflow participants.
motivation: Current durable-execution frameworks centralize authoritative workflow state with the hosting provider, raising trust, control, and availability concerns.
method: It designs single-writer epoch cores, quorum-finalized closure certificates, explicit certificates for durability/timeout/checkpoint decisions, and a separate content-addressed payload distribution plane, along with a threat model and typed invariants.
result: The proposal distinguishes what signatures establish from what they do not and defines prototype experiments, including adversarial cases, to validate or falsify its central mechanisms.
conclusion: The work is a distributed-systems architecture proposal for durable workflow state, not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Ghost-Filled Orders: Detecting And Testing Atomicity Violations In Non-Custodial Prediction Markets
authors: Zhiyang Chen, Fan Long, Zhendong Su
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blockchain based prediction markets combine offchain order management with onchain settlement. This architecture supports user controlled custody, since users keep funds in wallets or smart contracts while submitting signed orders to an offchain order book. However, it creates an atomicity gap. An order may be valid when accepted or matched offchain, but become invalid before the corresponding onchain settlement transaction is executed. This behavior, often called ghost filled orders by the community, can cause trades that appear filled offchain to fail onchain. This paper studies this atomicity gap through a case study of Polymarket. We show how the delay between offchain order acceptance and onchain settlement allows adversaries to invalidate unfavorable orders after observing market outcomes or price movements. We then quantify the scale and financial impact of this behavior over a nine-month period from August 12, 2025, to May 22, 2026, using 1.8 million reverted transactions involving Polymarket official smart contracts. Our analysis separates attacker profit from market and user loss, and develops conservative measurement rules to avoid overclaiming impact. We further develop a methodology for testing other blockchain based prediction markets and apply it to three additional markets. We find that all three are vulnerable to the same class of attack, and that one design enables direct attacker profit. We have reported the findings to all three projects; one project had acknowledged the issue at the time of the study.
tldr: This paper studies an atomicity gap in blockchain-based non-custodial prediction markets (e.g., Polymarket) where offchain-accepted orders can be invalidated before onchain settlement, enabling 'ghost-filled order' attacks.
motivation: Non-custodial prediction markets separate offchain order management from onchain settlement, which preserves user custody but introduces a window in which orders can become invalid after being matched offchain.
method: The authors perform a case study of Polymarket, analyze 1.8 million reverted transactions over a nine-month period, and develop conservative measurement rules to separate attacker profit from market and user loss, then apply the methodology to three additional markets.
result: Adversaries can exploit the delay between offchain acceptance and onchain settlement to invalidate unfavorable orders after observing market outcomes; all three additional markets tested were vulnerable, and one design permits direct attacker profit.
conclusion: Ghost-filled orders constitute a systemic atomicity vulnerability across blockchain prediction markets; the findings were disclosed to the affected projects, with one acknowledging the issue.

title: PentestChain: A Cost-Aware, MCP-Orchestrated Framework For Automated Penetration Testing With Free-Tier LLMs
authors: Rushabh Vipulkumar Patel, Dipo Dunsin, Mohammed Almaiah, Mohamed Chahine Ghanem
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-driven penetration testing has been demonstrated with premium frontier models such as GPT-4, but the per-engagement token cost makes continuous, automated testing unaffordable for the smaller organisations that need it most. This paper presents PentestChain, a ten-phase automated penetration testing framework that couples a curated, deterministic exploit map with a cost-aware AI cascade-a local Ollama model (qwen2.5-7b) first, then free-tier OpenRouter and Cerebras, with a rule-based fallback that always produces output-and exposes the full pipeline through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with eleven tools. We make three contributions. First, we treat US-dollar cost per engagement as a measured, first-class evaluation metric and show that a 7B-parameter local model, kept off the critical path by a deterministic backbone, sustains end-to-end operation at zero measured paid-API cost. Second, we analyse the attack surface that an MCP-exposed offensive engine introduces, grounding a four-position threat model in the 2025 MCP incident record (the CVE-2025-6514 remote-code-execution flaw in mcp-remote, the postmark-mcp supply-chain backdoor, and the tool-poisoning-rug-pull-line-jumping class), and contribute four mitigations. Third, we specify a reproducible, containerised evalua-tion protocol aligned with the standardised testbeds now expected at top-tier venues-AutoPenBench, a Cybench subset, and the PentestGPT 182-sub-task benchmark-with multi-trial statistics (more than 10 trials per configuration, pass-at-k, non-parametric significance tests and effect sizes) and direct, same testbed reproduction of the PentestGPT and PentestAgent baselines rather than citation of their published numbers. On the legacy targets measured to date, the framework detected 26 services, enriched 34 CVEs, produced.
tldr: PentestChain is a cost-aware, MCP-orchestrated automated penetration testing framework that uses free-tier and local LLMs with a deterministic exploit map to achieve zero measured paid-API cost.
motivation: AI-driven penetration testing is typically demonstrated with expensive frontier models, making continuous automated testing unaffordable for smaller organizations that need it most.
method: The framework uses a ten-phase pipeline with a curated deterministic exploit map and an AI cascade (local Ollama qwen2.5-7b, free-tier OpenRouter/Cerebras, rule-based fallback), exposed via an MCP server with eleven tools, plus a containerized evaluation protocol on AutoPenBench, Cybench, and PentestGPT benchmarks.
result: On legacy targets, the framework sustained end-to-end operation at zero measured paid-API cost, detected 26 services, enriched 34 CVEs, and produced outputs while analyzing MCP-related attack surfaces and mitigations.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that a 7B local model kept off the critical path by a deterministic backbone can make automated penetration testing affordable and reproducible, while also addressing the security risks of exposing an offensive engine through MCP.

title: Rational Reductions And Regular Languages Of Constant Circuit Complexity
authors: Amaldev Manuel Stefan G\"oller
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the circuit complexity of regular languages in terms of unbounded fan-in Boolean circuit families. We characterize the regular languages of constant circuit complexity in terms of the one-variable fragment of first-order logic with regular predicates, in terms of the pseudovariety of stamps [MATH], suitable word congruences and regular expressions. We analogously characterize the neutral letter regular languages of constant circuit complexity. Our lower bound result implies that the class of regular languages of sublogarithmic circuit complexity coincides with the one of constant circuit complexity. In addition we show that deciding whether a regular language, given as a nondeterministic finite automaton, has constant circuit complexity is [MATH]-complete. We introduce a strong notion of reduction, called rational truth-table reduction, that is tailored towards algebraically defined classes of languages. We show that, for a class of functions we call mild, rational truth-table reductions preserve both upper and lower bounds on circuit complexity. We show that the class of regular languages, whose circuit complexity is bounded by a mild function, is in fact a length-multiplying variety of languages. Slightly extending the class of regular languages of constant circuit complexity, we analogously characterize the class of regular languages that are in the pseudovariety [MATH]. For these we derive logarithmic circuit complexity upper bounds.
tldr: The paper characterizes regular languages of constant and sublogarithmic circuit complexity using one-variable first-order logic with regular predicates, word congruences, and pseudovarieties, and introduces rational truth-table reductions tailored to algebraically defined language classes.
motivation: Understanding the circuit complexity of regular languages bridges automata theory/algebraic language theory with Boolean circuit complexity, but existing characterizations lacked algebraic and logical descriptions of the constant-complexity class.
method: The authors use unbounded fan-in Boolean circuit families, the one-variable fragment of first-order logic with regular predicates, pseudovarieties of stamps, and a new notion of rational truth-table reduction preserving circuit-complexity bounds for 'mild' functions.
result: They show regular languages of sublogarithmic circuit complexity equal those of constant circuit complexity, prove that deciding constant circuit complexity for a given NFA is complete for a certain complexity class, and characterize a related pseudovariety with logarithmic circuit complexity upper bounds.
conclusion: The work provides algebraic, logical, and expression-based characterizations of low-complexity regular languages and a reduction framework suitable for algebraically defined language classes, all within classical automata and circuit complexity theory.

title: Robot Visions: Breaking reCAPTCHA At Zero Cost And Zero Shot
authors: Samantha Gottlieb Suphannee Sivakorn
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Google reCAPTCHA is the most widely deployed visual CAPTCHA service, protecting hundreds of thousands of websites from automated bots. It serves as a critical line of defense against automated attacks, including credential stuffing, bulk account creation, and automated form abuse. It has proven largely effective since its introduction in 2007. However, the rise of accessible AI now threatens its efficacy. Prior work has demonstrated that commercial cloud-based vision-language models (VLMs) can solve visual CAPTCHA challenges, but at non-trivial monetary cost per attempt. In this paper, we show that free and locally-run models can break Google reCAPTCHA. We conduct a comprehensive study of reCAPTCHA and present a taxonomy of its challenge types: Type A (independent image tiles, with static and dynamic sub-variants) and Type B (a single image partitioned into a 4x4 grid), each demanding a distinct solving strategy. We design zero-shot, no-cost solvers built entirely on open-source local models, specifically CLIP (58% per-challenge accuracy on Type A) and OWLv2 (43.5% on Type B), requiring no model training and no API access. Our end-to-end automated solver achieves a 92.6% per-session success rate across 500 real-world reCAPTCHA sessions. We further demonstrate that reCAPTCHA can be defeated by a non-technical adversary, using only natural-language instructions to a commodity AI assistant. This collapses the practical attacker skill floor to near zero and fundamentally changes the threat model for challenge-based CAPTCHAs. Although reCAPTCHA increasingly favors reputation-based verification, visual challenge-based fallback persists as a safety net that, paradoxically, has become the weakest link in the defense chain, suggesting that challenge-based visual CAPTCHAs may have reached the end of their useful life.
tldr: Free, locally-run open-source vision-language models (CLIP, OWLv2) can solve Google reCAPTCHA challenges zero-shot with a 92.6% per-session success rate, collapsing the attacker skill floor.
motivation: Google reCAPTCHA is a widely deployed defense against automated abuse, and prior work showed that only costly commercial cloud VLMs could break it, leaving the question of whether free local models suffice unanswered.
method: The authors build a taxonomy of reCAPTCHA challenge types (Type A independent image tiles and Type B single-image 4x4 grid) and design zero-shot, training-free solvers using open-source CLIP and OWLv2 models in a fully automated pipeline.
result: CLIP achieves 58% per-challenge accuracy on Type A and OWLv2 43.5% on Type B, yielding an end-to-end 92.6% per-session success rate over 500 real-world reCAPTCHA sessions; a non-technical user can also defeat it via natural-language instructions to a commodity AI assistant.
conclusion: Visual challenge-based CAPTCHAs have become the weakest link in the defense chain and may have reached the end of their useful life, fundamentally changing the threat model for challenge-based CAPTCHAs.

title: Fully Differentiable Framework For Inverse Identification Of Geometry And Material Parameters With Application To Determining Stress-free Configuration Of Soft Tissues
authors: Hyunoh Bae (school Of Mechanical Engineering, Purdue University, West Lafayette, USA), Tianyi Hu (school Of Mechanical Engineering, Purdue University, West Lafayette, USA), Adrian Buganza Tepole (department Of Mechanical Engineering, Columbia University, New York, USA), Hector Gomez
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical images of soft tissues typically depict loaded configurations rather than true unloaded (stress-free) states, which can bias biomechanical simulations and inverse material identification. A gradient-based inverse finite element framework is presented that jointly reconstructs an effective unloaded reference geometry and estimates hyperelastic material parameters from two or more observed deformed configurations. The formulation is fully differentiable and leverages exact end-to-end gradients to enable unified, simultaneous optimization of geometry and constitutive parameters. The objective function combines a nodal-position misfit with a deformation-gradient-based mismatch term, improving robustness under large deformations. Benchmark studies quantify the influence of loading diversity and observation count and demonstrate reduced sensitivity to poor material initialization. Finally, application to an MRI-derived breast model shows accurate recovery of the unloaded configuration and constitutive parameters from multiple gravity-loaded states. The framework provides a unified and scalable tool for inverse biomechanics with potential applications in personalized modeling, elastography, and surgical planning.
tldr: A fully differentiable inverse finite element framework jointly reconstructs stress-free reference geometry and hyperelastic material parameters of soft tissues from multiple deformed configurations.
motivation: Medical images of soft tissues capture loaded rather than unloaded states, biasing biomechanical simulations and inverse material identification.
method: The authors formulate a gradient-based inverse finite element problem with exact end-to-end gradients, optimizing nodal-position misfit plus a deformation-gradient-based mismatch term over observed deformed states.
result: Benchmark studies quantify the effects of loading diversity and observation count, and an MRI-derived breast model accurately recovers the unloaded configuration and constitutive parameters.
conclusion: The framework offers a unified, scalable tool for inverse biomechanics with applications in personalized modeling, elastography, and surgical planning.

title: Shannon Entropy And Complex Network Community Detection To Study Electoral Coalition Behaviour At Municipal Scale
authors: Andrea Lo Sasso
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional electoral analyses often rely on aggregate sociopolitical indicators or on macroscopic models grounded in statistical physics that treat election data at national level; however, these models have rarely been applied to local-level voting data, where the analytical complexity is substantially higher. In this study, we propose a framework rooted in statistical physics and complex network theory to investigate the fine-grained architecture of voting behaviour at the local scale. Leveraging a granular dataset from the 2024 municipal and 2025 regional elections in Bari, Italy, we represent the urban electoral landscape as a complex network, in which polling sections are modelled as nodes connected by links that encode statistically significant correlations based on vote expression. For each coalition participating in the elections, community detection reveals geographically proximal clusters that transcend administrative boundaries. Furthermore, in order to quantify whether a coalition exhibits territorially homogeneous voting behaviour or, instead, is fragmented into distinct voting blocs, we adapt latent-ideology estimation and the information-theoretic Shannon entropy [MATH] to the intra-coalition scale. Our results indicate that winning coalitions exhibit significantly higher territorial fragmentation, and these findings suggest that, at the local level, electoral success is not driven by the maintenance of geographically uniform consensus rather than by the capacity to aggregate diverse and non-homogeneous voting blocs. This scalable, data-driven framework moves beyond simple geographic accounting, providing a robust tool for uncovering the structural dynamics of political idea clustering and coalition fragmentation in complex urban environments.
tldr: The paper applies Shannon entropy and complex-network community detection to municipal-scale electoral data from Bari, Italy, to characterize territorial fragmentation of political coalitions.
motivation: Traditional electoral analyses rely on aggregate sociopolitical indicators or macroscopic statistical-physics models at the national level, and rarely address fine-grained local voting data where complexity is much higher.
method: Polling sections are modeled as nodes in a correlation-based complex network, community detection identifies geographically proximal clusters, and latent-ideology estimation combined with information-theoretic Shannon entropy quantifies intra-coalition territorial homogeneity versus fragmentation.
result: Winning coalitions exhibit significantly higher territorial fragmentation, suggesting electoral success at the local level stems from aggregating diverse, non-homogeneous voting blocs rather than maintaining geographically uniform consensus.
conclusion: The scalable, data-driven framework offers a robust tool for uncovering structural dynamics of political-idea clustering and coalition fragmentation in urban environments.

title: Geometric Hybrid Dynamical Systems: Part I - Modeling And Stability
authors: Piyush P. Jirwankar, Daniel E. Ochoa, Ricardo G. Sanfelice
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a framework for the modeling and analysis of geometric hybrid dynamical systems as hybrid inclusions on [MATH]-manifolds. Using tools from nonsmooth and set-valued analysis on manifolds, we derive coordinate-independent sufficient conditions for the existence of nontrivial solutions to this type of systems. We present geometric notions of uniform stability and attractivity of compact sets, and establish their equivalence to metric-based stability notions when the manifold is endowed with a Riemannian structure. We also introduce nonsmooth Lyapunov functions and a hybrid Lyapunov theorem providing sufficient conditions for uniform global asymptotic stability of compact sets. Finally, by characterizing [MATH]-limit sets of precompact solutions, we derive a hybrid invariance principle for geometric hybrid dynamical systems. The results are demonstrated through several running examples.
tldr: The paper develops a coordinate-independent framework for modeling and analyzing hybrid dynamical systems (hybrid inclusions) on smooth manifolds, including Lyapunov stability theorems and an invariance principle.
motivation: Hybrid systems—combining continuous evolution with discrete jumps—have been well studied in Euclidean spaces, but a fully geometric, coordinate-independent treatment on manifolds with rigorous stability theory was lacking.
method: The authors use nonsmooth and set-valued analysis on manifolds to define hybrid inclusions, derive sufficient conditions for existence of nontrivial solutions, define geometric notions of uniform stability and attractivity, and prove a hybrid Lyapunov theorem and invariance principle via omega-limit sets.
result: They show geometric stability notions coincide with metric-based ones on Riemannian manifolds, obtain Lyapunov sufficient conditions for uniform global asymptotic stability of compact sets, and characterize precompact solutions' limit sets to yield a hybrid invariance principle.
conclusion: The framework provides a rigorous geometric foundation for hybrid dynamical systems on manifolds, illustrated with running examples, with the caveat that interpretation depends on the manifold's metric structure.

title: Fourier Decay Of Srb Measures For Skew Products
authors: Haojie Ren Ga\'etan Leclerc
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Fourier decay of natural invariant measures for real analytic skew products [MATH] on [MATH], where [MATH] is expanding and [MATH]. Let [MATH] denote the associated solenoidal attractor. We prove a dichotomy: either [MATH] is a single horizontal graph, or both the SRB measure and the measure of maximal entropy have polynomial Fourier decay. No transversality assumption is imposed.
tldr: The paper proves a dichotomy for Fourier decay of SRB measures and measures of maximal entropy for real analytic skew products on the torus, without transversality assumptions.
motivation: Fourier decay of invariant measures is central to understanding mixing and spectral properties in dynamical systems, especially for skew products where standard transversality conditions may fail.
method: The authors analyze real analytic skew products over an expanding map and study the associated solenoidal attractor using techniques from analytic number theory and ergodic theory.
result: They show that either the attractor is a single horizontal graph, or both the SRB measure and the measure of maximal entropy exhibit polynomial Fourier decay.
conclusion: This provides a strong dichotomy for Fourier decay in a non-transversal setting, advancing the understanding of natural invariant measures for skew products.

title: The Complexity Of Finding Stationary Points In Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization
authors: Guy Kornowski
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17780v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that first-order algorithms require [MATH] gradient queries (in the worst case) to find a [MATH]-Goldstein stationary point of a Lipschitz function, at which there is a convex combination of gradients within distance [MATH] whose norm is at most [MATH]. This lower bound is tight, matching known algorithms up to absolute constants, therefore resolving the complexity of convergence to stationarity in nonsmooth nonconvex optimization. We further prove a tight lower bound of [MATH] for finding points satisfying the recently proposed relaxed notion of [MATH]-stationarity, which allows combining further-away gradients. Our results reveal that convergence rates to nonsmooth stationarity are not affected by gradient stochasticity, in sharp contrast to smooth optimization.
tldr: The paper resolves the worst-case complexity of finding Goldstein stationary points in nonsmooth nonconvex optimization by proving tight first-order oracle lower bounds.
motivation: Convergence to stationarity in nonsmooth nonconvex optimization lacked a matching lower bound, leaving the fundamental query complexity of the problem open.
method: The author establishes worst-case lower bounds on the number of gradient queries required by first-order algorithms to reach an ε-Goldstein stationary point of a Lipschitz function, and extends the analysis to the relaxed δ-stationarity notion.
result: First-order algorithms require Ω(ε^{-3}) gradient queries for ε-Goldstein stationarity, matching known upper bounds up to constants, with a tight analogous bound for relaxed stationarity; the rates are unaffected by gradient stochasticity.
conclusion: The complexity of convergence to nonsmooth stationarity is now settled, highlighting a sharp contrast with smooth optimization where stochasticity degrades rates.

title: A Variational Mollification Approach To Circular Deconvolution
authors: Mirza Karamehmedovi\'c, Pierre Mar\'echal, Mykhailo Petrov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a variational mollification approach to circular deconvolution based on the reconstruction of a mollified target object rather than the exact solution itself. The method is formulated as a convex variational problem whose solution admits an explicit Fourier representation. We establish the consistency of the proposed reconstruction as the target resolution increases and derive convergence rates for deterministic data perturbations. For ordinary smooth kernels, the method achieves the classical order-optimal algebraic convergence rates under Besov-Nikolskii smoothness assumptions, while for supersmooth kernels it attains the corresponding order-optimal logarithmic rates. Numerical experiments on synthetic and wind-direction data illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and confirm the theoretical predictions.
tldr: The paper proposes a convex variational mollification method for circular deconvolution that reconstructs a smoothed target object with explicit Fourier representation, achieving order-optimal algebraic and logarithmic convergence rates for ordinary and supersmooth kernels respectively.
motivation: Deconvolution of circular data is ill-posed and standard approaches struggle to balance stability against resolution; the authors aim for a principled variational formulation that offers provable convergence guarantees.
method: They cast the reconstruction as a convex variational problem in Fourier space, reconstructing a mollified target rather than the exact solution, and analyze consistency plus convergence rates under Besov-Nikolskii smoothness for deterministic perturbations.
result: The method attains classical order-optimal algebraic rates for ordinary smooth kernels and order-optimal logarithmic rates for supersmooth kernels, verified by numerical experiments on synthetic and wind-direction data.
conclusion: Variational mollification provides a theoretically sound and practically effective framework for circular deconvolution across different kernel smoothness regimes.

title: Day-ahead Coordination Of Virtual Power Plants Within Active Distribution Networks Using Deterministic Bi-Level Optimization
authors: Laura M. Barajas-Arguello, Rafael A. N\'u\~nez-Rodr\'iguez, Daniel Gebbran, Clodomiro Unsihuay-Vila
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a deterministic bilevel optimization framework for the coordinated operation of Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) embedded in an active distribution network. The Distribution System Operator (DSO) acts as the upper-level leader, minimizing a weighted combination of expenditure, active losses and voltage deviation subject to nonlinear AC power flow constraints, while each VPP operates as a lower-level follower that maximizes its profit under the uniform price signal issued by the DSO. Unlike most existing formulations, which linearize the lower-level subproblem to obtain a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP), the proposed model retains the full AC Optimal Power Flow (AC-OPF) equations, producing a bilevel Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Program (MINLP). The lower-level problem is replaced by its Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) optimality conditions and the Strong Duality Theorem, yielding a single-level Mathematical Program with Equilibrium Constraints (MPEC). Complementarity conditions are then linearized via the Fortuny-Amat big-M transformation. The framework is validated on the IEEE 33-bus feeder over a 24-hour horizon, with four distributed resources aggregated into a single VPP. Compared with individual dispatch against a regulated time-of-use tariff, aggregation reduces active losses by 10.5 %, the accumulated voltage deviation by 18.3 %, and the bus-hours below 0.95 p.u. from 132 to 29. These gains cost 0.31 % in social cost and 0.26 % in DSO expenditure, while the rent of the aggregator is preserved.
tldr: The paper proposes a deterministic bilevel optimization framework for day-ahead coordination of Virtual Power Plants within an active distribution network, retaining full nonlinear AC power flow constraints.
motivation: Existing VPP coordination formulations typically linearize the lower-level problem into a MILP, which sacrifices accuracy in representing the AC power flow physics of the distribution network.
method: A bilevel MINLP is formulated with the DSO as upper-level leader (minimizing cost, losses, and voltage deviation) and each VPP as lower-level follower (maximizing profit); the lower level is replaced by its KKT conditions and strong duality to yield an MPEC, with complementarity conditions linearized via the Fortuny-Amat big-M transformation.
result: On the IEEE 33-bus feeder over 24 hours with four DERs aggregated into one VPP, aggregation reduced active losses by 10.5%, accumulated voltage deviation by 18.3%, and bus-hours below 0.95 p.u. from 132 to 29, at a cost of 0.31% in social cost and 0.26% in DSO expenditure while preserving aggregator rent.
conclusion: The framework demonstrates that AC-accurate bilevel coordination of VPPs can deliver meaningful network performance gains with modest economic trade-offs, offering a practical alternative to linearized MILP approaches.

title: The Natural Components Of An Autoregressive Time Series On Banach Space
authors: Brendan K Beare Phil Howlett
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that an autoregressive time series on Banach space can be canonically identified with a finite direct product of self-contained and self-determined natural components defined on separate subspaces by the spectral projections for each spectral point of the characteristic linear pencil. We assume the resolvent of the pencil is analytic everywhere except for the spectral points which may be poles or isolated essential singularities. Each natural component is represented as a forward, backward or outward flow fixed by an upstream boundary condition in the far distant past, the far distant future, or at a nominated initial time---depending on whether the corresponding spectral point is outside, inside, or on the unit circle.
tldr: The paper shows that an autoregressive time series on a Banach space decomposes canonically into self-contained natural components defined on spectral subspaces determined by the spectral points of the characteristic linear pencil.
motivation: Autoregressive models are typically studied in finite-dimensional Euclidean settings; extending them to Banach spaces requires understanding how spectral structure governs the decomposition of the process.
method: Using spectral projections of the characteristic linear pencil, whose resolvent is assumed analytic away from spectral points (poles or isolated essential singularities), the process is decomposed as a finite direct product of natural components on separate subspaces.
result: Each natural component is represented as a forward, backward, or outward flow depending on whether its spectral point lies outside, inside, or on the unit circle, fixed by an upstream boundary condition in the past, future, or at a nominated initial time.
conclusion: The decomposition provides a canonical spectral characterization of Banach-space autoregressive time series, clarifying how boundary conditions select the appropriate flow for each component.

title: Remembering Solomon Marcus
authors: Florin Nichita
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18224v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: From the manifest of Andre Breton, through the transdisciplinary understanding, we arrive at a post-modern manifest. A talk by Laura De Marco (Harvard) will provide scientific background to approach an AMS poetry. The next section will be a qualitative analysis of some new operations on the real numbers. The conclusions will be given in the last section, and an appendix will recall some previous work with some new comments.
tldr: A memorial/reflective piece honoring Solomon Marcus, touching on transdisciplinary thought, an arts-and-sciences poetry talk, and some new operations on real numbers.
motivation: The author aims to commemorate Solomon Marcus and reflect on his transdisciplinary legacy, connecting literary manifestos with mathematical and scientific ideas.
method: Qualitative and discursive exposition: narrative recollection, discussion of a talk by Laura De Marco, and an informal analysis of novel operations on real numbers.
result: No formal theorem or quantitative result is established; the contribution is a qualitative discussion plus an appendix revisiting previous work with new comments.
conclusion: The paper is a commemorative and philosophical piece rather than a technical contribution, offering reflections rather than advancing any specific research program.

title: Near-Optimal Deterministic Exact-Value Complexity For Smooth Convex Optimization
authors: Wendao Wu, Haihan Zhang, Chenheng Zhang, Yanyi Li, Chunyuan Zheng, Cong Fang, Haoxuan Li, Zhouchen Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the deterministic oracle complexity of smooth convex optimization when the algorithm receives only exact function values. The objective is a globally [MATH]-smooth convex function, all queries and the final output are restricted to the Euclidean ball of radius [MATH], and the unique minimizer lies in the ball of radius [MATH]. We establish an upper bound of [MATH] using coordinate finite differences together with an error-robust accelerated projected method. Our main contribution is a matching lower bound, up to the high-accuracy saturation of the construction: any deterministic adaptive value-oracle algorithm requires [MATH] queries. Consequently, the minimax oracle complexity is [MATH] throughout the moderate-accuracy regime [MATH] for a universal constant [MATH]. The lower bound must account for the fact that a single exact real value can encode arbitrarily much information. To overcome this difficulty, we construct a single fixed smooth convex hard instance using a Moreau-smoothed biased max chain, an exact prefix-shielding mechanism, and batched delayed rotations. These techniques preserve consistency with the full adaptive transcript and establish the optimality of the square-root complexity branch for deterministic bounded-query algorithms.
tldr: This paper establishes matching upper and lower bounds on the deterministic oracle complexity of smooth convex optimization when only exact function values (not gradients) are available.
motivation: Derivative-free/value-only optimization is important when gradients are unavailable, but the deterministic minimax complexity of the exact-value oracle model was not tightly characterized in the moderate-accuracy regime.
method: The authors use coordinate finite differences combined with an error-robust accelerated projected method for the upper bound, and construct a hard instance via a Moreau-smoothed biased max chain, exact prefix-shielding, and batched delayed rotations to prove the lower bound.
result: They obtain a square-root dependence on accuracy throughout the moderate-accuracy regime and prove a matching lower bound, showing a single exact real-value query can encode arbitrarily much information yet cannot beat the derived complexity.
conclusion: The minimax oracle complexity for exact-value smooth convex optimization is settled (up to high-accuracy saturation), establishing optimality of the square-root complexity branch for deterministic bounded-query algorithms.

title: Decentralized Optimal Equilibrium Learning Over Dynamic Networks
authors: Muhammed O. Sayin Seref Taha Kiremitci
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies decentralized learning of socially optimal equilibria in finite normal-form games over dynamic communication networks. Each agent observes only its own realized payoffs, does not know the game a priori, and can communicate only with time-varying neighbors using low-bandwidth messages. We propose networked decentralized optimal equilibrium learning dynamics in which agents generate randomized semantic content/discontent signals from local payoff comparisons and exchange time-stamped time-stacked tables rather than raw actions, payoff information or local estimates/parameters. The method combines table fusion with temporal majority reconstruction to mitigate dynamic communication while preserving fully decentralized operation. We establish finite-time logarithmic regret guarantees, with an in-phase exploration perturbation, for optimal equilibrium selection under utilitarian and proportional-fair social welfare objectives. Simulation results further show that the proposed approach can effectively select socially desirable equilibria over dynamic communication networks.
tldr: The paper proposes decentralized learning dynamics that let agents in a finite normal-form game converge to socially optimal equilibria over time-varying low-bandwidth communication networks.
motivation: Agents often lack a priori knowledge of the game and can only observe local payoffs while communicating with changing, bandwidth-limited neighbors, so fully decentralized equilibrium selection is needed.
method: Agents exchange randomized semantic content/discontent signals derived from local payoff comparisons using time-stamped, time-stacked tables combined with table fusion and temporal majority reconstruction.
result: The authors prove finite-time logarithmic regret guarantees with in-phase exploration perturbation for utilitarian and proportional-fair welfare objectives, and simulations confirm effective equilibrium selection.
conclusion: Decentralized table-based signaling enables robust socially optimal equilibrium learning under dynamic, low-bandwidth network conditions.

title: Learning Market Competition In Shared Spectrum: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
authors: Randall Berry Qixuan Zai
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates market competition among wireless service providers (SPs) that serve customers using shared spectrum. Prior work has analyzed such markets through models of competition with congestible resources, capturing both the congestion-sensitive nature of wireless spectrum and the effects of spectrum sharing on service quality. These models typically assume that the market demand function is known, enabling SPs to optimize pricing or quantity decisions under either Bertrand or Cournot competition. In contrast, we consider a setting in which the demand function is initially unknown and must be learned over time. We model this learning process using multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), allowing competing SPs to learn market dynamics while adapting their competitive strategies. Although MARL has shown strong performance in a variety of economic settings, recent work has demonstrated that it can also give rise to tacit collusion among self-interested agents. We therefore examine whether similar collusive behavior emerges in shared-spectrum markets and how its prevalence depends on the mode of competition (price versus quantity) and the choice of MARL algorithm. Our results provide insight into the interaction between learning dynamics, market structure, and spectrum sharing, with implications for both wireless market design and the deployment of learning-enabled decision-making systems.
tldr: This paper uses multi-agent reinforcement learning to study market competition among wireless service providers sharing spectrum, focusing on whether tacit collusion emerges when the demand function is unknown and must be learned.
motivation: Prior shared-spectrum market models assume the demand function is known, so providers can immediately optimize pricing or quantity decisions; the authors ask what happens when demand must instead be learned over time by competing agents.
method: Competing service providers are modeled as agents in a multi-agent reinforcement learning setting under Bertrand (price) and Cournot (quantity) competition, and the learned dynamics are examined for emergent collusive behavior across different MARL algorithms.
result: The results characterize how the prevalence of tacit collusion depends on the mode of competition (price versus quantity) and the specific MARL algorithm used, revealing interactions among learning dynamics, market structure, and spectrum sharing.
conclusion: The findings offer implications for wireless market design and for the deployment of learning-enabled decision-making systems in shared-spectrum environments.

title: Bridging The Opacity: Evidence-Backed Cross-Chain Transaction Correspondence Reconstruction Across Heterogeneous Blockchains
authors: Dan Lin, Huan Xiao, Ziwei Li, Xiapu Luo, Jiachi Chen, Jiajing Wu, Zibin Zheng
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross-chain bridges enable interoperability, but they also break the transaction trails needed to trace illicit funds. Third-party investigators typically cannot access the source-to-destination mappings maintained by bridge backends, and our survey of 131 bridges finds that only 16.79% provide complete public tracking. Existing approaches depend on official APIs, EVM-specific assumptions, or fragile temporal heuristics, limiting their ability to trace transfers across heterogeneous ledgers. We present XSplicer, an evidence-driven system for reconstructing cross-chain transaction correspondence (xTCR) without privileged access to bridge backends. XSplicer derives unified semantic specifications from public protocol documentation and transaction examples, translates them into lightweight parsers and verifiers, and links source and destination transactions by prioritizing hard evidence and using soft clues only when necessary. We evaluate XSplicer on seven bridge protocols spanning EVM, Bitcoin, and Solana. XSplicer achieves 92.5% global recovery rate and up to 98.61% on individual protocols. Under adversarial noise, its hard-evidence verifier retains the correct match in 100% of tested cases, while soft-clue matching degrades as ambiguity increases. In two real-world case studies, XSplicer recovers more than 1,900 historical transaction pairs after Multichain ceased operations and identifies 754 illicit cross-chain transfers worth 105.6 million USD in the Bybit laundering incident. These results show that public protocol invariants can support practical cross-chain forensics without privileged bridge mappings.
tldr: XSplicer reconstructs cross-chain transaction correspondence without privileged bridge access by extracting public protocol invariants and linking source-destination transactions using hard evidence and soft clues.
motivation: Cross-chain bridges break transaction trails, and most bridges lack public tracking APIs, hindering forensic tracing of illicit funds across heterogeneous ledgers such as EVM, Bitcoin, and Solana.
method: The system derives unified semantic specifications from public protocol documentation and examples, translates them into lightweight parsers and verifiers, and matches transactions by prioritizing hard evidence with soft clues only when necessary.
result: XSplicer achieves 92.5% global recovery and up to 98.61% on individual protocols across seven bridge protocols, retains 100% hard-evidence match accuracy under adversarial noise, and recovers over 1,900 historical pairs plus 754 illicit transfers worth $105.6M in case studies.
conclusion: Public protocol invariants can enable practical cross-chain forensics without privileged bridge mappings, offering a robust alternative to API-dependent or heuristic tracing methods.

title: Autonomy In Check: Governor-Mediated Adaptive Security At The Edge
authors: Ijaz Ahmad, Ijaz Ahmad, Flavio Esposito, Erkki Harjula
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adaptive security at the network edge increasingly relies on automated planners, including rule-based controllers, learned policies, and LLM-assisted agents, that translate observations into enforcement actions. Once such a planner can influence live policy state, syntactic validity is not enough. A semantically wrong action, produced from incomplete or manipulated observations, can be faithfully executed by an enforcement substrate that cannot judge mission context. We address this problem by treating the boundary between planner output and kernel enforcement input as the primary security object. We propose a split-control architecture in which an untrusted planner emits typed security intents, a deterministic governor checks each intent against safety, resource, temporal-stability, and proportionality invariants, and only admitted actions are bound to signed receipts and compiled into pre-installed eBPF map updates. The paper formalizes this trust-boundary problem, defines three threat classes, develops the governor admission predicate, and reports an end-to-end prototype. Across rule-based and LLM-assisted planners on a Raspberry Pi 5 testbed connected to the university 5G Test Network, the governor admits, rejects, and bounds intents at microsecond cost without disrupting protected-flow regularity. The contribution is conceptual as much as empirical: adaptive security does not need to trust the author of an action. It needs a mediation boundary that decides whether the action is admissible.
tldr: The paper proposes a split-control architecture where an untrusted planner emits typed security intents that a deterministic 'governor' validates against safety, resource, temporal-stability, and proportionality invariants before compilation into eBPF map updates at the network edge.
motivation: Adaptive edge security increasingly uses automated planners (rule-based, learned, or LLM-assisted) whose outputs are executed by enforcement substrates that cannot judge mission context, so syntactically valid but semantically wrong actions can be faithfully carried out. The authors argue the planner-to-kernel boundary itself should be the primary security object.
method: The work formalizes the planner/enforcement trust-boundary problem, identifies three threat classes, and defines a deterministic governor admission predicate checked against safety, resource, temporal-stability, and proportionality invariants. Admitted actions are bound to signed receipts and compiled into pre-installed eBPF map updates.
result: An end-to-end prototype evaluated on a Raspberry Pi 5 testbed connected to a university 5G test network shows the governor admits, rejects, and bounds intents at microsecond cost for both rule-based and LLM-assisted planners without disrupting protected-flow regularity.
conclusion: Adaptive security does not need to trust the author of an action; it needs a mediation boundary that decides admissibility, which the governor-based split-control design provides.

title: MiST: Mid-Training LLMs For Cybersecurity
authors: Oded Ovadia, Elad Ben Zaken, Elad Guttman, Orly Moreno Kadosh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cybersecurity combines high-stakes analysis with complex technical language, making it an impactful and challenging domain for LLMs. We present MiST (Mid-trained Security Transformer), a suite of 8B and 32B models that achieve strong performance on public cybersecurity benchmarks. We use mid-training as an intermediate adaptation stage between general pre-training and cybersecurity training. Rather than performing continual pre-training over large volumes of raw domain text, we curate a compact, expert-vetted seed corpus, and transform it into high-quality domain-specific synthetic training data. The final MiST checkpoints improve mean cybersecurity accuracy by +13.1 and +8.6 absolute percentage points over the corresponding Qwen baselines for 8B and 32B, respectively, corresponding to relative gains of +27.0% and +15.8%. Ablation results further show that these cybersecurity gains arise in the mid-training and supervised fine-tuning stages through a combination of the synthetic data generation flows. Furthermore, we show that MiST provides a stronger initialization for downstream task-specific fine-tuning adaptation and reinforcement learning.
tldr: MiST is a suite of 8B and 32B LLM checkpoints adapted for cybersecurity via a mid-training stage using a curated, expert-vetted seed corpus expanded into synthetic domain data.
motivation: Cybersecurity analysis demands both high-stakes reasoning and complex technical language, making it a challenging but impactful domain for LLM specialization beyond general pre-training.
method: Rather than continual pre-training on massive raw domain text, the authors use 'mid-training' as an intermediate adaptation stage, converting a compact expert-curated corpus into high-quality synthetic cybersecurity training data before supervised fine-tuning.
result: MiST improves mean cybersecurity benchmark accuracy by +13.1 and +8.6 absolute points (+27.0% and +15.8% relative) over Qwen baselines at 8B and 32B, and provides a stronger initialization for task-specific fine-tuning and RL.
conclusion: Mid-training with curated synthetic data is an effective, efficient route to domain-specialized LLMs, yielding transferable gains for downstream adaptation.

title: Modelling Sexual Partnership Dynamics And Population Heterogeneities In Agent-based Dynamic Network Models
authors: Priyanka Nair-Turkich, Patricia T. Campbell, Nicholas Geard
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Population-level heterogeneities, combined with temporal fluctuations in sexual partnerships, shape the structure of sexual contact networks and can substantially influence the spread of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Traditional static network models, which assume fixed attributes of partnerships, such as count and duration, may not adequately capture the effects of partnerships on STI transmission. In contrast, agent-based dynamic network models offer a flexible framework for incorporating individual and population-level heterogeneities. We developed an agent-based dynamic network model in which partnership formation and dissolution probabilities, stratified by age, sex, and sexual orientation (including bisexual individuals), govern the formation of monogamous and concurrent partnerships and their dissolution via a duration-dependent hazard. Partnership statistics from the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (NATSAL-3) were used as model calibration targets, and Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) was used to generate candidate parameter combinations. Parameter estimation was performed by selecting the combination that produced the lowest Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the model outputs and the calibration targets. Our study addresses three questions: (1) how well can the observed characteristics of sexual partnerships in NATSAL-3 be reproduced using an agent-based model; (2) how does concurrency shape the structure of dynamic sexual contact networks; and (3) how do concurrent partnerships affect the dynamics of STI transmission. In this study, we find that interactions between individual characteristics such as age, sex, and sexual orientation, and partnership attributes such as count, duration, and concurrency play a critical role in shaping the population-level sexual contact network and, in turn, the dynamics of STI transmission.
tldr: An agent-based dynamic network model calibrated to NATSAL-3 data reproduces sexual partnership statistics and shows how concurrency and population heterogeneities shape STI transmission dynamics.
motivation: Traditional static network models assume fixed partnership attributes such as count and duration, which may inadequately capture how temporal partnership dynamics and individual heterogeneities affect STI spread.
method: The authors built an agent-based dynamic network model where partnership formation and dissolution probabilities are stratified by age, sex, and sexual orientation, with duration-dependent hazard for dissolution; parameters were calibrated to NATSAL-3 targets via Latin Hypercube Sampling and MSE minimization.
result: The model reproduces observed partnership characteristics from NATSAL-3 and demonstrates that concurrency, interacting with age, sex, and sexual orientation, strongly shapes network structure and STI transmission dynamics.
conclusion: Interactions between individual characteristics and partnership attributes are critical in shaping population-level sexual contact networks and should be captured by dynamic rather than static network models of STI spread.

title: Why Some Strikes Last Longer: The Resilience Paradox Of Partially Functional Institutions
authors: Nuno Crokidakis
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Labor strikes do not necessarily lead to complete institutional disruption, particularly when non-striking sectors maintain part of normal activities. We propose a minimal dynamical model to investigate how such residual activity affects the persistence of labor conflicts. The model couples strike participation, institutional response, and overall functionality through two competing mechanisms: a direct suppressive effect of residual activity on strike participation and an indirect effect arising from the reduced institutional pressure to resolve the conflict. Analytical calculations reveal a counterintuitive regime in which increasing residual activity increases, rather than decreases, stationary strike participation. We characterize this behavior through a strike-response susceptibility and derive an exact compensation threshold separating the conventional regime from a resilience-paradox regime. At the threshold, the two mechanisms exactly balance, making stationary strike participation independent of residual activity. Numerical results confirm the analytical predictions and illustrate the underlying mechanism. Our results show that institutional resilience can have an unintended dynamical consequence: by absorbing part of the disruption generated by a strike, continued operation may reduce the urgency of institutional response and thereby favor conflict persistence. This provides a simple example of how individually stabilizing processes can collectively generate counterintuitive outcomes in complex social systems.
tldr: A minimal dynamical model shows that residual institutional activity during labor strikes can counterintuitively increase stationary strike participation via a resilience paradox.
motivation: Strikes often do not fully disrupt institutions because non-striking sectors sustain partial activity, yet how this residual activity affects conflict persistence is unclear.
method: The authors couple strike participation, institutional response, and overall functionality through two competing mechanisms—direct suppression of participation by residual activity and indirect reduction of institutional pressure to resolve the conflict—and analyze the model analytically and numerically.
result: Analytical calculations reveal a counterintuitive regime where more residual activity increases stationary strike participation, with an exact compensation threshold separating conventional from resilience-paradox behavior, confirmed numerically.
conclusion: Institutional resilience can have the unintended dynamical consequence of favoring conflict persistence, illustrating how individually stabilizing processes can produce counterintuitive collective outcomes in complex social systems.

title: Optimal Control Via Chemotactic Sensitivity Of A Logistic Keller-Segel Model
authors: Yacouba Simpore, Mahamadi Warma, Luis P. Yapu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.18030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study an optimal control problem for a two-equations Keller-Segel system on a bounded domain with Neumann boundary conditions, where the chemotactic sensitivity is modulated by a control [MATH] acting on the taxis flux [MATH]. We prove the well-posedness of the state equation under low regularity assumptions. The analysis is based on the study of an [MATH]-regularized problem, the application of Schauder's fixed point theorem, [MATH]-independent, positivity and a priori estimates, the passage to the limit as [MATH], and a uniqueness argument. For a cost functional combining trajectory tracking, taxis penalization, control regularization, and terminal objectives, we establish the existence of optimal controls and derive the first-order optimality conditions through a Lagrange multiplier framework, leading to an adjoint system and a variational inequality for the optimal control. A numerical scheme based on spline collocation in space and Runge-Kutta time-stepping is set and implemented. Numerical experiments are performed to simulate the free and controlled dynamics in conservative and non-conservative cases.
tldr: The paper studies an optimal control problem for a two-equation logistic Keller-Segel chemotaxis system where the chemotactic sensitivity is modulated by a control acting on the taxis flux.
motivation: Keller-Segel systems model chemotaxis-driven aggregation, and controlling the chemotactic sensitivity offers a handle on pattern formation and blow-up behavior in such biological transport models.
method: The authors prove well-posedness of the state equation under low regularity via an ε-regularized problem, Schauder's fixed point theorem, positivity and a priori estimates, then establish existence of optimal controls and first-order optimality conditions through a Lagrange multiplier framework leading to an adjoint system and variational inequality; numerics use spline collocation in space and Runge-Kutta time stepping.
result: Existence of optimal controls is established along with adjoint-based first-order necessary optimality conditions, and numerical experiments simulate free and controlled dynamics in conservative and non-conservative regimes.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous optimal-control framework for chemotaxis models with controlled sensitivity, but it lies entirely in applied PDE analysis and biological modeling with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Reflections On Trusting Trust, Revisited: Contaminating Self-Modifying Ai Coding Agents With Poisoned Benchmarks
authors: Tadayoshi Kohno Franziska Roesner
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thompson's "Reflections on Trusting Trust" showed that a compiler can be poisoned to reinsert its own backdoor, so that even recompiling clean source reproduces the Trojan. Today, substantial coding work is done by AI coding agents -- and increasingly, those agents generate new versions of themselves. We reconsider Thompson's attack when the "compiler" is a self-modifying coding agent. Can an adversary supply poisoned benchmarks to the agent's self-evaluation and self-improvement process to induce future versions of the agent to write vulnerable code on clean, held-out tasks? We instantiate this attack against three recently proposed self-modifying coding agents: the Darwin G\"odel Machine (with our experimental modifications), the Self-Improving Coding Agent, and Hyperagents (both substantively unmodified). We demonstrate successful proofs-of-concept: for example, with Hyperagents powered by Sonnet 4.5, our poisoned benchmark leads the agent to self-evolve instructions that disable HTTPS certificate validation on neutral URL-fetching tasks. From our experiments, we distill properties of the vulnerability, benchmark, model, and agent scaffolding that are sufficient to enable a benchmark poisoning attack. Moreover, we show that contamination often persists even when a poisoned agent is subsequently evolved against clean benchmarks. We discuss defensive directions and argue that self-modifying coding agents must be designed to be more resilient to such attacks.
tldr: The paper revisits Thompson's 'Trusting Trust' attack in the context of self-modifying AI coding agents, showing that poisoned benchmarks can induce future agent versions to write vulnerable code.
